item.title: Ratko Mladic, former general convicted of Bosnia genocide, dies
item.description:
PEOPLE-RATKO MLADIC/

Ratko Mladic, convicted of genocide for orchestrating the 1995 massacre of at least 8,000 Muslims in a U.N.-designated "safe area" of Bosnia, Europe's worst atrocity since World War Two, died on Thursday in U.N. custody.

The slaughter in Srebrenica was the grisly culmination of a war that had lasted over three years, in which the general pounded the besieged capital Sarajevo daily with the artillery, tanks, mortars and heavy machineguns of his nationalist Serb army, killing 10,000.

The dead from Srebrenica were bulldozed into mass graves over four days in July 1995, some of them dug up and relocated to remote mountains so as to hide evidence of the killings.

The goal, as determined by the United Nations International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY), was "ethnic cleansing" — the forcible expulsion of Bosnian Muslims, Croats and other non-Serbs to clear Bosnian lands for a Greater Serbia.

The tribunal found that Mladic, together with late Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic and Bosnian Serb political leader Radovan Karadzic, were part of a criminal conspiracy to implement the plan.

"I do not recognise this court," Mladic, dubbed the "Butcher of Bosnia" by his opponents, said at an ICTY hearing on his case in 2014. When he was sentenced to life in prison in 2017 he shouted: "This is all lies, you are all liars!"

Mladic died in U.N. custody on Thursday, his lawyer Dragan Ivetic said, without giving a cause. He had spent his last months in the hospital ward of the U.N. detention centre holding him in a suburb of The Hague, Ivetic added.

According to his son, documents gave Mladic's date of birth as 12 March 1942, but he was actually born on 8 March 1943.

'Germans had Hitler, Serbs have Mladic'

Karadzic, also convicted of genocide in 2016, and Mladic topped the ICTY wanted list for years after Western powers ended the war. But until Milosevic was toppled by a popular uprising in 2000, Mladic lived securely — if discreetly — in Belgrade.

Milosevic died in detention on 11 March 2006, a few months before a verdict in his four-year tribunal trial for genocide and other war crimes in Croatia, Bosnia and Kosovo.

The army Mladic created to fight in Bosnia was a model of ruthlessness, daring and brutality in the Serb warrior tradition, once prized in the life-or-death partisan struggle against the Nazi occupation of Yugoslavia in World War Two.

In some of the most horrific examples, prisoners suffocated in the heat after being forced to eat salt and denied water; were starved and raped in prison camps; were made to jump off a bridge and shot; and were gunned down at night by the hundreds after being driven out of detention with chemical gas.

"For me Mladic is a symbol of all horrible crimes that happened during the war — our girls were raped, and boys killed, only because they were Muslim," said Munira Subasic, whose son and husband were killed by Bosnian Serb forces after they overran Srebrenica.

"Germans had Hitler, Serbs have Mladic," Subasic continued. "There is no difference between the two."

Mladic had a cameraman film the blitz on the encircled enclave of Srebrenica, to show him extolling his "lads" and haranguing Dutch U.N. peacekeepers who misguidedly accepted his solemn word that the inhabitants would be safe in his hands. Srebrenica supposedly had "safe area" status, meant to protect civilians from ethnic cleansing.

"We give this town to the Serb people as a gift," Mladic said to the camera, claiming the victory as revenge against Muslim Turks, who once held the area as part of the Ottoman Empire.

The next day, Mladic's forces were filmed handing out sweets to children, promising their safe passage. Meanwhile, thousands of men and boys were being readied for execution.

When NATO tried in 1995 to rein in his forces with the threat of limited air strikes, his troops defiantly seized U.N. peacekeepers as human shields, chaining them to likely targets.

In November 1996 Mladic and top generals gave in to strong Western pressure that he step down as ordered by Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic, who succeeded Karadzic and was later jailed for her role in war crimes.

Son of partisan fighter

The son of a World War Two partisan fighter killed in 1945, Mladic was an officer in the old communist Yugoslav People's Army (JNA) when Yugoslavia's disintegration began in 1991.

When Bosnian Serbs rose in 1992 against Bosnia's Muslim-led secession, Mladic was picked to command the new Bosnian Serb army that swiftly overran 70 per cent of the landlocked country.

Dozens of towns were besieged with heavy weapons that once belonged to the JNA and villages were burned down as 22,000 troops of the U.N. Protection Force stood by more or less helplessly, with orders not to take sides.

A combination of Western pressure, covert American arms and training for Croats and Muslims gradually turned the tide against Mladic's army. Determined NATO strikes did the rest.

Sick and frail

Despite Western appeals, the reformists ruling Serbia after Milosevic's fall did not dare move against a man who was a hero to a core of nationalist Serbs.

Sporadic sightings put him at a Belgrade horse race or a soccer match. In 2004, NATO said he had toasted hard-drinking old comrades at his former bunker in Han Pijesak, Bosnia.

When he was finally arrested in 2011, he put up no resistance. His right arm was lame, the apparent result of an untreated stroke. He looked nothing like the burly general in camouflage who ruffled the hair of a Srebrenica boy in 1995.

He suffered a heart attack in 2013 and seemed older than his years. By his own account, he felt like a frail old man.

In his few court appearances, he wavered between self-pity, smiling defiance and vague distraction.

"I am a very sick man," Mladic pleaded to the court.

In 2019, Mladic told the judges that he was too ill to participate in outdoor exercises and requested leave to visit the graves of family members in Serbia. The request was denied.

His appeal against conviction was rejected in 2021, as were repeated requests for his release on compassionate grounds.

In August 2026, a U.N. doctor found Mladic's death "may occur at any time," possibly within weeks, but his application for release was again rejected as not in the interests of justice.

item.title: CNG pressure improves Friday after month-long gas shortage
item.description:
After nearly a month of severe gas shortages, CNG-powered vehicle drivers in Dhaka saw some relief on Friday, with improved gas pressure at filling stations.
While CNG autorickshaw drivers had recently been able to get only Tk 40–60 worth of gas, they managed to fill up to Tk 150 on Friday. Private car owners also got Tk 300–350 worth of gas. However, long queues at CNG stations remained.
Drivers and CNG station workers said a CNG autorickshaw can normally take up to Tk 600 worth of gas, depending on its cylinder size. Private cars with 60-litre cylinders can take around Tk 600 worth, while those with 90-litre cylinders can take up to Tk 1,000.
According to sources, Dhaka has been facing a severe gas shortage for nearly a month. Many filling stations stopped selling CNG due to insufficient gas pressure, while those still operating could provide only Tk 40–60 worth of gas per vehicle. Drivers often had to wait in line for hours even for that amount.
However, gas pressure improved somewhat on Friday. Although long queues remained, CNG drivers were able to get more than Tk 100 worth of gas, while private cars received around Tk 350 worth.
CNG autorickshaw driver Sushil Kumar said he waited for about an hour at a filling station in Hazipara, Rampura, in the morning and got Tk 120 worth of gas. Later, after joining another queue around 12:30pm, he waited until 2pm to get Tk 140 worth.
“Even with more than Tk 100 worth of gas, I can make two or three trips, or up to four if they are short. But with less than Tk 100 worth, I have to return for gas after just two trips,” he said.
“Getting this much today is better than nothing. But our situation has become so difficult that it is hard to support our families,” he added.
Another CNG driver, Musa, said he waited for about one and a half hours in Demra early in the morning before getting gas. He then drove to Uttara, followed by trips to Banani and Dhanmondi, before going to Moghbazar shortly after noon for another refill, where he got Tk 150 worth of gas.
“I earned Tk 1,200 from three trips, but spent around Tk 400 on expenses. If I can earn another Tk 1,000–1,200 by the evening and night, that should be enough,” he said.
“Today’s gas supply was manageable, but we don't know what will happen tomorrow,” Musa added.
Private car driver Yunus said gas pressure was noticeably better on Friday.
“Earlier, I could not get more than Tk 120 worth. Today, I got Tk 350 worth, which is still good,” he said.
He said his car could normally take Tk 600 worth of gas, but he was able to get Tk 350 on Friday.
“Even this is not bad. If the situation remains like this, we can at least make some trips. But with only Tk 120 worth of gas, I cannot travel to Narayanganj and return. That is why we are afraid to take our cars outside the city,” he said.
Meanwhile, better gas pressure was reported at several stations in Badda, Uttara, Khilkhet and Mirpur.
Jamil, an employee at Zaman CNG station in Badda, said, “The pressure seems somewhat better today, Friday. But we cannot say what it will be like tomorrow.”
Ibrahim, an employee at a CNG station in Hazipara, said, “Gas pressure has increased somewhat today. We are able to supply gas. There are still queues, but drivers are getting gas because the pressure has improved.”

item.title: Two arrested over hacking of man in Mohammadpur
item.description:
Police have arrested two people over the hacking of an Bangladeshi expatriate in Mohammadpur, Dhaka, reportedly stemming from his relationship with his former wife.
The arrestees are Shanto and Billal alias Kala Billal. Police said they are members of a teen gang.
DMP Mohammadpur Zone Additional Deputy Commissioner (ADC) Jewel Rana disclosed the information at a press briefing at Mohammadpur police station around on Friday.
He said the victim, Laskar Hridoy, was hacked and injured in the Mohammadpur Limited area. His father filed a case at Mohammadpur police station over the incident.
Four members of a local teen gang were named in the case: Munna alias Captain Munna, Russell alias Anda Russell, Billal alias Kala Billal and Garhkata Saiful. Several others were also named as unidentified accused.
ADC Jewel said police launched an operation after the case was filed and arrested two members of the teen gang. Billal alias Kala Billal was arrested late Thursday night (August 27).
He said a love triangle was mainly behind the incident.
According to the police official, Hridoy married a woman named Hafsa Akter several years ago. A few days after their marriage, Hafsa developed a relationship with teen gang leader Captain Munna.
She later eloped with Munna and married him. Three years later, Hridoy went to Saudi Arabia.
Despite leaving the country, Hridoy continued communicating with Hafsa and allegedly maintained a secret relationship with her.
After learning about the relationship, Munna called Hridoy and warned him against talking to Hafsa, while also issuing various threats. Despite this, Hridoy and Hafsa continued communicating, police said.
Hridoy recently returned to Bangladesh on vacation. After learning of his return, Munna allegedly called him on Monday and hacked him, leaving him seriously injured.
Hridoy was attacked just three days after returning to the country.
He is currently undergoing treatment at a hospital.

item.title: Chinese rescuers reach main site of deadly Tibet mudslide
item.description:
Chinese rescuers faced treacherous conditions on Friday as they reached the main area wiped out by a deadly mudslide at the Tibet-Nepal border to search for hundreds of missing people, state media reported.
Two days after Tibet’s border trade hub of Gyirong was pummeled by a wall of mud and debris, a team of 21 rescuers became the first to reach it in the late afternoon on Friday, state news agency Xinhua said.
Chinese President Xi Jinping chaired a meeting of top leaders about rescue operations, as the death toll in Tibet rose to five, with 558 still missing.
“There are still many hidden dangers of glaciers, ice lakes and geological disasters in the surrounding area, and rescue is facing great difficulties,” Xinhua reported the leaders as saying.
After the mudslide hit on Wednesday, a huge lake formed upstream, raising concerns that it could burst and cause further severe flooding.
But risks from that lake are “gradually decreasing,” Chinese state media reported on Friday, adding that rescue operations were “proceeding in an orderly manner.”
Authorities had earlier paused operations in the worst affected area, citing the risk of renewed flooding due to the lake water beginning to overflow, state broadcaster CCTV said.
Later, a CCTV report said water from the lake was “flowing out naturally, with the outflow discharge exceeding the inflow discharge.”
“Compared to the high water level in the early morning on August 27, the lake’s water level has dropped by around 10 meters (33 feet), and the risk is gradually decreasing,” it added.
It was not immediately clear if the lake was the same as a debris dam that Nepalese authorities warned had burst on Friday.
Family members of the missing were being housed in the area by authorities as they waited for news, one woman told AFP.
She said she had not been able to reach her relative, a police officer at Gyirong, or his wife, since the disaster happened, and had been told he was missing by his work unit.
CCTV said that 499 Chinese nationals and 555 foreigners had been transported out of the disaster zone as of Friday.
Rescue workers are using drone-based 3D modelling and thermal imaging detection, as well as manual searches, to locate those still missing, said CCTV.
Xi offered Beijing’s help in Nepal’s rescue operations, in a condolence message to the country’s president.
“China is willing to actively assist Nepal in its rescue efforts and provide support and aid to the best of its ability,” Xi said according to CCTV.

item.title: Vegetable prices fall as fish, meat, eggs remain costly
item.description:
Some relief has returned to the capital’s kitchen markets as prices of several vegetables have fallen amid increased supply, though high prices of eggplant, tomatoes and beans continue to keep overall market costs elevated.
Papaya is now the cheapest vegetable at Tk30 per kg, while pointed gourd, okra, spiny gourd, ridge gourd and jali are selling for around Tk60 per kg, according to visits to several markets in the capital on Friday.
Bitter gourd is selling for Tk70 per kg, while bottle gourd and snake gourd cost Tk80. Common cucumbers are available for Tk50-60 per kg, while local cucumbers are more expensive at Tk80-100.
However, eggplant and tomato prices remain high. Long eggplant is selling for Tk100 per kg, round eggplant for Tk120, and tomatoes for Tk120-140.
Beans are among the most expensive vegetables, with prices ranging from Tk180 to Tk200 per kg depending on the market.
Green chilli prices have also fallen somewhat amid increased supply and are now selling for Tk120-140 per kg, depending on quality.
Pintu Mia, a shopper, said the lower prices of some vegetables had brought some relief.
“Several vegetables are now within our reach, with different varieties available for Tk60-80. This has reduced our market expenses somewhat. However, some vegetables are still expensive,” he said.
Another shopper, Jewel Sheikh, said the overall cost of shopping had not fallen significantly despite lower prices for some vegetables.
“Papaya, pointed gourd, okra and ridge gourd are comparatively cheap. But if eggplant and tomato prices also fell, ordinary consumers would get more relief,” he said.
Traders attributed the decline in prices of some vegetables to increased supply, while saying limited supplies of eggplant and tomatoes were keeping their prices high.
Nasir Hossain, a vegetable seller at Rayshaheb Bazar, said the supply of pointed gourd, okra, ridge gourd and jali was currently good.
“We are selling these vegetables for around Tk60 per kg, while papaya is Tk30. But we have to buy eggplant and tomatoes at higher prices from wholesale markets, so we have to sell them at higher prices,” he said.
Nurul Islam, a seller at Narinda Kacha Bazar, said vegetables arriving in larger quantities had become cheaper.
“But the supply of eggplant and tomatoes is low, so there is little scope to reduce their prices,” he said.
Despite some relief in vegetable prices, the markets for fish, meat and eggs have remained largely unchanged over the past week.
Broiler chicken is selling for Tk190-200 per kg, while Sonali chicken costs Tk320-340.
Egg prices also remain high, with a dozen selling for Tk150 and four eggs for Tk50.
“Farm chicken eggs are now being sold for Tk150 per dozen,” said Masud, an egg seller.
Fish prices have also remained more or less unchanged. Tilapia is selling for Tk250-260 per kg, pangas Tk230-250, rohu and catla Tk380-420, and shrimp Tk1,000-1,300.
Pabda costs Tk350-400 per kg, large rohu Tk450-500 and tengra Tk700.
Vetki is selling for Tk400-550 per kg, mrigal Tk250-300, baim Tk600-800, local koi Tk700-800, farmed koi Tk300 and poa Tk260.
Farmed shing costs Tk300-450 per kg depending on size, while medium-sized rohu is selling for Tk300-350. Rupchanda, shol and river bele are priced at more than Tk1,000 per kg.
Fish seller Ujjal Hossain said prices fluctuate depending on supply and demand.
“Prices are lower when supply is high and rise when less fish arrives in the market. Similarly, prices increase when there are more buyers. So the price of the same fish can sometimes differ between morning and afternoon,” he said.
Aminul Islam, another shopper, said fish prices were still largely the same.
“Some fish are available at comparatively lower prices, but good-quality fish are much more expensive. It is becoming difficult to keep fish purchases within the family budget,” he said.

item.title: Anee urges opposition cooperation to rebuild Bangladesh
item.description:
Water Resources Minister Shahiduddin Chowdhury Anee has called for opposition cooperation to protect democracy and rebuild Bangladesh.
“The people have entrusted the BNP with running the country. Another party contested the election and is now in opposition, but did not attend our swearing-in ceremony or extend any cooperation. They are still threatening to launch a movement,” he said.
Anee made the remarks on Friday at an exchange meeting with beneficiaries of the SDF’s ‘Be Strong’ project in South Durgapur of Dighli Union under Chandraganj upazila in Lakshmipur.
He said the BNP had waged a 17-year movement against Sheikh Hasina and suffered losses during that period.
“Everyone joined the movement to save the country and protect democracy. Now our task is to safeguard those gains and build a new Bangladesh. We need the opposition’s cooperation for this,” he said.
Referring to the opposition’s long march and plans for further agitation, Anee said continued political unrest would hamper development.
“Such movements will harm both the local community and the country,” he said.
He alleged that the opposition was trying to weaken the BNP through street movements and urged everyone to remain united and work together to protect the government’s mandate.
Chandraganj Upazila Nirbahi Officer Nilufa Yasmin chaired the meeting, attended by local BNP leaders and officials, including Chandraganj police OC Abdur Rob, Upazila BNP President Belal Hossain and General Secretary Yusuf Bhuiyan.

item.title: Indian national held after border gunfight in Moulvibazar
item.description:
An Indian national was detained with a foreign-made pistol, two rounds of ammunition and 500 yaba tablets after a gunfight between the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) and a group of suspected Indian smugglers along the Barlekha border in Moulvibazar on Thursday night.
The detainee was identified as Bolai Das, who was detained in an injured condition following the gunfight, saidLt ColAtaur Rahman, commander of Biyanibazar Battalion (52 BGB).
He said the BGB had received confidential information that a group of Indian smugglers was attempting to bring firearms and drugs into Bangladesh through the Kumarshail border area of Barlekha.
Acting on the information, a special BGB patrol team took position in the Kumarshail area and launched an operation around 10pm on Thursday (August 27).
When the suspected smugglers were challenged, they opened fire at the BGB personnel, prompting the border guards to return fire in self-defence, the BGB official said.
The other members of the group managed to flee, while Bolai Das was detained in an injured condition.
A search of his belongings led to the recovery of the foreign-made pistol, two rounds of ammunition and 500 yaba tablets,Lt ColAtaur said.
Bolai Das is currently receiving treatment under BGB custody, while legal proceedings against him are underway.
Meanwhile, BGB patrols and intelligence surveillance have been strengthened along the border to prevent smuggling and illegal entry, the official said.

item.title: Neighbor sent to jail over alleged rape of six-year-old
item.description:
A Dhaka court on Friday sent Sumon Mia, a neighbor to jail over the alleged rape of a six-year-old child in Dhaka’s Shah Ali police station area.
Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Mohammad Ismail passed the order following an application by the investigation officer in the case.
Shah Ali Police Station Sub-Inspector (SI) Osman Gani, the investigation officer, produced Sumon before the court and sought an order to keep him in jail.
Sub-Inspector Ila Moni of the prosecution department said there was no bail application on behalf of the accused. The court subsequently ordered him to be sent to jail.
Police arrested Sumon from a residence near the Shah Ali Royal City Pocket Gate at around 8pm on Thursday.
Niaz Mehedi, additional deputy commissioner of the Dhaka Metropolitan Police’s Media and Public Relations Division, citing police and the police station, said: “A complaint was received that the child had been raped in the area at around 4:30pm on Wednesday.”
“Later, the child’s mother took her to Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital. After examination, doctors suspected that the child might have been raped. She was then referred to Dhaka Medical College Hospital for advanced treatment.”
Niaz Mehedi further said: “When the child’s mother asked her, she mentioned Sumon, a tenant in the neighboring house.”
“The child alleged that Suman took her to his room and raped her.”
The child’s mother filed a case at Shah Ali Police Station on Thursday in connection with the incident.

item.title: Kamrangirchar Loha Bridge reopens after 25-day renovation
item.description:
Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) has reopened the Kamrangirchar Loha Bridge after completing renovation work in 25 days with its own funding.
DSCC Administrator and freedom fighter Md Abdus Salam inaugurated the renovated bridge on Friday, with Dhaka-7 MP Hamidur Rahman attending as the special guest.
The 145-metre-long and 4.2-metre-wide bridge is used by around 70,000 people every day. The renovation is expected to benefit nearly 5 million residents of Kamrangirchar.
The renovation of the dilapidated bridge is expected to ease travel difficulties for local residents and pedestrians while improving safety.
Speaking at the inauguration, DSCC Administrator Md Abdus Salam said the city corporation was committed to making travel easier and safer for city residents.
He said completing the renovation in a record 25 days with DSCC’s own funding demonstrated that commitment.
Salam said an initiative had also been taken to revise the proposed eight-lane project to preserve the historic bridge for future generations.
He announced that the bridge would henceforth be open only to pedestrians.
DSCC Region-3 Executive Engineer Ahsan Habib, officials concerned and local dignitaries were present at the inauguration.

item.title: Dhaka-Mawa Expressway sees 548 accidents since Padma Bridge opening
item.description:
A total of 548 road accidents have occurred on the Dhaka-Mawa Expressway since the Padma Bridge was opened on June 25, 2022, leaving 147 people dead and 874 injured, according to fire service sources.
Muhammad Shafiqul Islam, deputy assistant director of Munshiganj Fire Service and Civil Defense, said the accidents occurred between the Mawa Toll Plaza and Dhaleshwari Toll Plaza of the Dhaka-Mawa Expressway.
He said that from June 25, 2022 to Thursday, August 27, 2026, a total of 548 road accidents were recorded on the stretch.
Fire service firefighters risked their lives to rescue the injured and send them to hospitals, Shafiqul said. They also recovered the bodies of those killed and handed them over to police.
He said the number of road accidents is increasing alongside growing vehicle pressure on the Dhaka-Mawa Expressway.
In this situation, drivers and the general public need to become more aware to prevent accidents, he said.
Shafiqul also urged drivers to refrain from risky overtaking, follow road instructions and traffic signals properly, and drive within the prescribed speed limit.
He added that drivers should obey traffic laws, maintain a safe distance and refrain from inattentive and reckless driving to help reduce road accidents on the Dhaka-Mawa Expressway.

item.title: Moving beyond Dhaka’s shadow
item.description:
Dhaka stands as the undisputed epicentre of Bangladesh, concentrating within its own boundaries an overwhelming share of the nation’s chances, institutions, and essential services. U niversities, advanced medical facilities, key government ministries, corporate headquarters, and big financial institutions are all in the capital.
I n contrast, district and divisional towns increasingly look mostly abandoned, left out. Their economies stay stagnant, infrastructure lags, and even more, a steady stream of eager young people migrate to Dhaka for a better future.
This lopsided development pattern has turned the capital into a magnet that pulls resources from every corner of the country, while the outer areas get weakened and not properly served.
Every year hundreds of thousands of migrants show up, mainly because comparable opportunities elsewhere are in short supply, or just don’t exist.
This hyper concentration exacts a profound toll on both the capital and the nation. Dhaka’s roads and its public transport systems buckle daily under unbearable traffic congestion, wasting countless productive hours. Housing prices have climbed way past the reach of ordinary citizens, pushing many into overcrowded slums or informal settlements with minimal basic services.
Air pollution often reaches hazardous levels, posing serious threats to public health. Water supply and waste management systems struggle to keep up, while green spaces are shrinking rapidly. These pressures not only reduce the quality of life for residents, but also gradually erode the very attractiveness that once made Dhaka the preferred destination.
The consequences extend well beyond the city limits. A student from Barishal or a patient from Rangpur often faces arduous journeys, lengthy delays, and significant expenses to access quality higher education or specialized healthcare. Government services, business registrations, and even routine administrative approvals frequently require travel to or coordination through Dhaka, breeding inefficiency and frustration.
Talented professionals in fields such as medicine, engineering, teaching, and public administration show reluctance to serve in regional postings. They know that career advancement, superior schools for their children, and access to modern amenities remain overwhelmingly centred in the capital. As a result, smaller towns experience a steady brain drain that further stifles local innovation and growth.
Regional inequality seems to get worse, year after year. You can see it clearly in higher poverty levels, weaker education results in some places, and uneven access to electricity, sanitation, and even digital connectivity.
As this goes on, whole communities end up losing their most skilled people, and that quietly erodes local administration as well as economic energy. In the end, the country pays for it -- through human potential that stays unused and chances for broader, more inclusive progress that never quite happen.
Decentralization represents far more than a policy preference and stands as the only sustainable pathway to address these structural distortions. By genuinely transferring administrative, financial, and decision-making authority to divisional and district levels, Bangladesh can begin to distribute opportunities more equitably and alleviate the unsustainable load on Dhaka.
International stories provide valuable instruction. Countries in Southeast Asia and constituents in Europe demonstrate how devolved power, coupled with robust accountability mechanisms, can unleash capacity without sacrificing country-wide coordination.
Bangladesh, with its massive youth population and growing financial system, has the demographic to replicate such success. What remains critical is regular political commitment and effective implementation.
Some observers express the position that decentralization can lead to coordination problems, poor oversight, or adjacent capacity agility. These are valid points, but the status quo is not working, gripped with severe bottlenecks, bureaucratic delays, and coordination screw-ups on a nationwide scale.
The answer is pairing decentralization with capacity-building programs for neighbourhood administrations, transparent performance-based investments, strengthened oversight frameworks and anti-corruption safeguards.
The benefits would be far-reaching. An additional balanced cityscape will reduce environmental pressures, enhance the livability among us, and allow every citizen the chance to succeed no matter the place of birth.
Reduced migration can help the social fabric in rural and small metropolitan clusters, and inject clean dynamism into local economies. Strong nearby governance can also enhance responsiveness to climate challenges, which disproportionately affect different parts of the nation.
Continued over-reliance on a single, overburdened metropolis alongside the neglect of vast regional potential is neither desirable nor tenable in the long run. The evidence from population trends, economic data, and lived experiences all point in one direction. There is simply no viable alternative to genuine decentralization.
Md Ashikur Rahman is a development worker, and a graduate and postgraduate in public administration and governance studies.

item.title: Business schools need AI
item.description:
In Bangladesh, generative AI in business education is no longer a foreign trend arriving from North American campuses -- it's already in classrooms, WhatsApp groups, assignment drafts, and student presentations.
The real question isn't whether business schools should allow AI, but whether it will produce sharper thinkers or simply faster submitters.
The numbers frame why these matters. Bangladesh had 135.94 million internet subscribers as of June 2026 (BTRC), with 120.84 million connecting via mobile rather than fixed broadband.
Household internet access rose from 43.6% (2023) to 54.8% (2025); smartphone adoption climbed from 63.3% to 72.8% over the same period (BBS).
That's real progress, but a meaningful share of any classroom remains under-connected. Classroom capacity compounds this: UGC data puts Jagannath University's teacher-student ratio near 1:25 against an international benchmark of 1:20, while several Dhaka University departments routinely exceed 40-50 students per section.
Used well, AI can help a student unpack a dense case study in plain Bangla-English, rehearse a pitch, or organize field-interview questions in advance.
Bangladesh already has strong homegrown cases for this -- bKash reached roughly 84 million verified users by 2026; the country's mobile financial services processed an estimated 8.61% of global daily mobile money transactions in 2024 despite holding just 2.19% of the world's population.
Pathao reports over 600,000 jobs created (a company figure, not independently audited); ShopUp serves small neighborhood shops through commerce and logistics support.
But the line between support and substitution is everything.
Using AI to understand why bKash succeeded is learning. Submitting an AI-written assignment without field observation is outsourcing.
The distinction determines whether the tool builds capability or erodes it.
Adoption data shows this isn't evenly distributed. One study found ChatGPT usage among Bangladeshi students rising from 5% (2022) to 49% (2025), with a stark urban-rural gap: 78% versus 32%.
That overall figure still trails the roughly 71% global higher-education adoption rate reported by 2023-2024, suggesting Bangladeshi classrooms are unevenly saturated rather than over-saturated.
The stakes extend past grades.
ICT service exports reached $724.6 million in FY2024-25 (EPB), up 7.7% year-on-year, and Bangladesh hosts an estimated 650,000 active freelancers -- among the largest online-labour workforces globally per Oxford Internet Institute research.
The draft National AI Policy 2026-2030 explicitly directs education systems to guard against over-reliance, so students keep building core reasoning skills.
Assessment design should adapt accordingly: Pairing written work with vivas, reflection logs, field evidence, and AI-use declarations reward thinking over formatting.
Faculty need institutional support to make this shift, given already-stretched teacher-student ratios. Encouragingly, Brac University's 2026 cohort sent roughly 700 students into GCI World, a global AI education initiative spanning 114 countries, a sign infrastructure investment is underway, though it alone won't solve the assessment problem.
Bangladesh doesn't need graduates who submit just polished paragraphs but who can reason through messy realities. AI must be a tool for asking better questions, not skipping the struggle of answering them.
Dr Nusrat Hafiz is an Assistant Professor and Director, Women Empowerment Cell, Brac Business School, Brac University.

item.title: A record 129 failures: The agonizing timeline of the Sagar-Runi probe
item.description:
Investigating agencies in Bangladesh failed for a record 129th time yesterday to submit the probe report for the sensational double murder case involving the gruesome 2012 killing of journalist couple Sagar Sarowar and Meherun Runi inside the safety of their Dhaka home.
The incident immediately hogged the media spotlight and has never faded from public memory, particularly because the home minister at the time promised on camera to catch the killers within 48 hours.
By now, more than 127,000 hours have passed. Yet, agency after agency tasked by the government with investigating the murder has failed to produce a probe report.
The Sagar-Runi murder case now holds the record for the highest number of court hearing deferrals due to the non-submission of an investigation report, having been officially postponed 129 times.
While the Guinness World Records does not officially track this category, legal experts, human rights organizations, and media outlets widely cite it as an unprecedented anomaly in global judicial history.
This agonizing wait for justice has seen the couple’s minor son grow into an adult, traumatized by the fact that the killers remain unknown after 14 years.
Sagar Sarowar, a news editor for Maasranga Television, and his wife Meherun Runi, a senior reporter at ATN Bangla, were brutally murdered in their rented flat in West Rajabazar, Dhaka, on February 11, 2012, in the presence of their four-year-old son.
Over the past 14 years, the investigation has repeatedly changed hands, moving from the Detective Branch (DB) to the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB), and finally to the Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI). None of these shifts have yielded fruit.
Initially, the DB of the Dhaka Metropolitan Police was entrusted with the case before it was transferred to RAB. The elite crime-busting agency failed to submit its investigation report to the court, requesting extensions 111 times over 12 years.
On September 30, 2024, the High Court stripped RAB of its investigative authority. Three weeks later, the Ministry of Home Affairs formed a new high-powered task force, led by the PBI, to handle the investigation.
The High Court directed the authorities to complete the investigation and submit the report within six months, noting that the delay was a matter of regret not only for the victims' family but for every citizen. The court famously observed that "six months means six months."
The higher judiciary has previously noted that the delay in completing the investigation and commencing the trial is a continuous mockery of the justice system that damages the judiciary's reputation.
Public perception suggests that the sense of urgency and justice expressed by the higher judiciary is not reflected in the actions of the investigating agencies and government functionaries.
Requesting fresh extensions has become a ritualistic routine for these agencies, granting them a two-to-three-month respite before the cycle repeats.
No matter which agency takes the lead, the result remains the same: Endless delays and virtually zero new leads to pursue the perpetrators or formally begin the trial.
To break this decade-long deadlock, the High Court issued a series of binding directives. When the newly formed task force faced structural hurdles following the major political shifts in Bangladesh after August 5, 2024, the High Court granted a final six-month extension, ordering an unyielding submission.
In discussions about press gags and media intimidation in Bangladesh, the impunity surrounding this case remains a stark example of a hazardous working environment for journalists.
With an elected government now in power in post-February 2026 Bangladesh, fast-tracking this double-murder case is essential to restore faith in the country’s investigating agencies and pave the way for an intimidation-free media ecosystem.
Reaz Ahmad is Editor, Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Rangpur killings: Police vow to uncover motive, says new commissioner
item.description:
Rangpur Metropolitan Police (RPMP) Commissioner Mahbubur Rashid has vowed to uncover the actual motive behind the killing of four members of a family in the city and bring those responsible to justice.
The newly appointed commissioner made the remarks on Friday afternoon after inspecting the crime scene at Machuapara in Rangpur city.
“I came here to inspect the crime scene. The incident and the case are important. The investigation is ongoing. Many questions will arise during the course of the investigation, and it is our responsibility to find professional answers to those questions. We are working on that,” he said.
Mahbubur Rashid said the sensational killings were being investigated with the utmost importance and that police would examine all claims and information surrounding the case.
“There has been a lot of discussion across the country about this case. We want to collect evidence related to every claim and, through proper accountability, take the case to its logical conclusion and submit a charge sheet before the court so that justice can be ensured,” he said.
The commissioner also ruled out any negligence in investigating the case.
“All necessary technological and intelligence support is being used in the investigation. If any new clue emerges, let us know and we will investigate it. This is the job of the police, but we need cooperation from everyone,” he said.
Asked about allegations by the family of accused Siddhartha Das that police had washed the roof of teacher Ganapati Chakraborty’s house with water and destroyed evidence, the commissioner said he had also heard the allegation.
“I only joined in Rangpur yesterday. There is nothing to wash away from the evidence. It is a crime scene, and the evidence has been collected,” he said.
The investigation into the high-profile case has meanwhile been transferred from Kotwali Police Station to the Detective Branch (DB).
Zinat Ali, officer-in-charge of the Metropolitan Police Detective Branch, has been appointed as the new investigating officer.
Mahbubur Rashid also said drug abuse was not only a problem in Rangpur but a national social problem.
“I sat with my officers this morning and discussed the issue with them. I have given them some time. Hopefully, you will see a change within a week,” he said.
The four members of the family were found dead at their home in Daspara, Machuapara, in the Kamal Kachna area of Rangpur city.
On Saturday night, August 22, Puja Chakraborty called her sister Pritilata Chakraborty. When her sister’s phone was switched off, she called her brother-in-law, their daughter and their son one after another. All of their phones were also found switched off.
Puja then went to her sister’s house. After receiving no response despite calling at the gate, she informed police.
Police later went to the house and recovered the bodies of retired teacher Ganapati Chakraborty Jewel, 65, his wife Pritilata Chakraborty Bhola, 50, their postgraduate student daughter Agami Chakraborty Prarthi, 25, and their fifth-grade student son Ayush Chakraborty Priyam, 12.
Two men, Mugdha Das, 23, son of Kanudas, and Siddhartha Das, 19, son of Binay Chandra Das, were detained from the same area early Sunday morning.
The bodies were handed over to the family members on Sunday afternoon after autopsies. Their last rites were later performed at around 10:30pm at the Dakkhiganj cremation ground in the city.
On Sunday afternoon, Gopinath Chakraborty, elder brother of one of the victims, filed a murder case at Kotwali Police Station against unidentified persons.
Later that night, the two accused reportedly confessed to the killings before a court in statements recorded under Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. They were subsequently sent to jail.

item.title: High paddy seedling prices put farmers in distress
item.description:
Farmers in Sonatala upazila of Bogra are facing growing difficulties as the prices of Aman paddy seedlings have surged in local markets, despite ample supplies. They have urged the authorities to take immediate steps to keep paddy seedling prices within an affordable range.
During visits to several markets, including Syed Ahmed College Haat, Karamja Haat, Thakurpara Sanyasi Mela Haat, Velurpara Haat, Karpur Haat, Balua Haat, Harikhali Haat, Tekani Chukainagar Haat and Pakulla Haat, large quantities of paddy seedlings were found being brought in for sale.
Seedlings of BRRI Dhan-28, 29, 89 and 92, as well as Ranjit and various local varieties, were available. Eighty bundles were selling for Tk 350 to Tk 400. Seedlings of aromatic white- and black-grain varieties were considerably more expensive, with 80 bundles priced at Tk 700 to Tk 800.
Farmers said many of their own paddy seedlings had been damaged by prolonged dry weather, excessive heat, inadequate rainfall and irrigation shortages. As a result, they have been forced to depend on market-bought seedlings for Aman cultivation.
They also alleged that some traders and seedling producers were exploiting the increased demand to charge higher prices. According to farmers, the prices of paddy seedlings have risen nearly two to three times compared with last year.
Abdul Alim, a farmer from Padmapara village, said his seedbed dried up despite repeated irrigation efforts. “I could not save my seedlings despite providing irrigation and trying to protect them from the intense heat. I had no option but to come to the market, but the prices are too high,” he said.
Farmers Rafiqul Islam, Mozammel Haque and Bokul Pramanik of Thakurpara said rising diesel and irrigation costs had increased seedling production expenses. They added that paddy seedlings had also been damaged in some low-lying areas after fields were inundated.
Sonatala Upazila Agriculture Officer Krishibid Sohrab Hossain said the agriculture office was providing farmers with necessary technical advice to ensure successful Aman cultivation in line with the production target.
“Market monitoring is being strengthened to prevent paddy seedling shortages and ensure the sale of quality seedlings at reasonable prices,” he said.

item.title: Tk1,000cr spent, yet no end to Bhabodah waterlogging
item.description:
Despite more than Tk1,000 crore being spent on various projects over the past four decades, the Bhabodah region in Jessore is once again reeling from severe waterlogging, with more than a hundred villages submerged following days of continuous rain.
At Sujatpur village of Manirampur upazila, housewife Bithi Rani was desperately trying to save her family and belongings as rainwater entered her home. Recent rains had also submerged the fields, fish enclosures and roads, she said.
“There is waist-deep water in the yard, while the cowshed and kitchen are also flooded. We have moved our cattle to a higher road and are spending nights in a makeshift shelter there. Cooking has become extremely difficult. We are living with our children amid water, snakes and insects. How long will we have to live like this?” she asked.
Her suffering is shared by thousands of residents across Bhabodah. Continuous rainfall has inundated more than 100 villages in Manirampur, Keshabpur and Abhaynagar upazilas. Homes, schools, roads and religious institutions have gone underwater, forcing many families to take shelter on elevated roads with their livestock.
Locals estimate that around 80,000 people are currently waterlogged in several unions of the three upazilas. Thousands of fish enclosures have also been inundated. Shortages of safe drinking water, cattle feed and proper sanitation have made the situation increasingly difficult.
The latest crisis has raised fresh questions over the effectiveness of government initiatives. A Tk140 crore project launched in 2025 to dredge 81.5 kilometres of the Hori and Bhadra rivers had raised hopes of a lasting solution. However, recent rainfall has once again exposed the region’s vulnerability.
Residents blame the worsening situation on the failure to renovate the Amdanga Canal and inadequate drainage through sluice gates and rivers. They said a work order for the canal was issued two years ago, but work has yet to begin. The canal could potentially drain nearly 25% of Bhabodah’s water.
The river dredging project is also incomplete. Locals allege that a temporary embankment south of Kharnia Bridge and accumulated silt have obstructed water flow, worsening the waterlogging.
Iqbal Kabir Zahid, chief adviser to the Bhabodah Water Drainage Struggle Committee, said more than 200 villages across Jessore, Khulna and Satkhira had been inundated. He demanded immediate completion of the Amdanga Canal renovation, removal of temporary embankments and silt, phased implementation of Tidal River Management (TRM), and emergency food and healthcare support for affected people.
Jessore Water Development Board Executive Engineer Palash Kumar Banerjee said the obstruction near Kharnia Bridge had been removed and three sluice gates had been opened. More gates would be opened soon, he said, adding that water was draining rapidly.
Bhabodah covers parts of Abhaynagar, Manirampur and Keshabpur in Jessore and parts of Dumuria and Phultala in Khulna. Local activists say dredging alone cannot solve the crisis and that a coordinated, and long-term drainage plan is essential.

item.title: Three luxury cars seized in Cox’s Bazar over alleged import scam
item.description:
The Customs Intelligence and Investigation Directorate (CIID), Chittagong Regional Office, has seized three luxury cars in Cox’s Bazar over allegations that they were imported as parts and later assembled locally into complete vehicles.
The seized vehicles are a Toyota Supra, a Honda Civic and a Mazda MX-5.
Acting on a tip-off, a CIID team conducted a raid near the Ocean Paradise Hotel and Resort on Kolatoli Road in Cox’s Bazar on the night of August 27 and seized the three vehicles.
According to the CIID, the vehicles were allegedly brought into the country by declaring them as parts and were later assembled locally as complete cars.
During the operation, CIID officials also found that the vehicles were carrying markings reading “SINH4”, “S4FIAT” and “ESH4H” instead of conventional registration number plates.
The vehicles were seized under Section 191 of the Customs Act, 2023, pending verification of their import documents, ownership, customs declarations, payment of duties and taxes, and the legality of their local assembly, said a press release issued by the NBR.
The authorities suspect that the vehicles may have been imported by declaring different components as parts rather than as complete vehicles.
The investigation will determine whether the actual nature of the goods was concealed, false or incorrect declarations were made, or customs duties and taxes were evaded.
Section 33(2) of the Customs Act, 2023, may also be applicable if it is found that false information, statements or documents, or collusion, resulted in lower assessment of customs duties or charges or an erroneous refund.
If the investigation establishes that the vehicles were imported under the guise of other goods or through false or incorrect declarations, action will be taken under the relevant provisions of the Customs Act, 2023.
Five people have been identified as being linked to the vehicles: Hasibur Rahman Sinha of Cox’s Bazar, Azmain Raihan and Sharafat Rahman of Gazipur, and Nakibul Hasan and Sifiat Mahmud of Dhaka.
However, the investigation is still underway, and the authorities are verifying the ownership of the vehicles, their use, the individuals’ involvement in the import process and their roles.
Investigators will also determine how the different components entered Bangladesh and where and how they were subsequently assembled into complete vehicles.

item.title: ‘Ran for our lives:’ Tales of survival from Nepal-China disaster
item.description:
Some survivors of the deadly floods on the Nepal-China border ran for their lives, others narrowly missed disaster, but all were eyewitnesses to a major calamity and its aftermath.
Rescue crews in helicopters have been plucking survivors from along the valleys ravaged in the tsunami-like flow of water and debris apparently unleashed by a glacier’s collapse.
More than 1,400 people were still missing on Friday -- many of them foreign tourists -- and over 550 people were dead.
Here is what survivors told AFP:
Sivaranjani Muthunathan was travelling in Nepal by bus with 56 others from India’s southern state of Tamil Nadu. They were heading towards the Chinese border when they became stuck in what they thought was a traffic jam.
“Then there was fog, smoke, something that seemed to suddenly engulf us,” Muthunathan, 46, told AFP, showing a video she recorded on her phone of a torrent surging towards her.
Vehicles were swept away or buried under mud around them.
“One by one, we also climbed out through the driver’s side,” she said, recounting how she had then scrambled up a hill.
Another pilgrim who was on the bus, 53-year-old Vijayabhuvaneshwari, said: “We had no choice.”
“Every vehicle in front of us, behind us, was gone,” she told AFP.
“As we were climbing up, we could hear what felt like explosions,” she said, giving only one name. “They were rocks and boulders crashing.”
With older members of the group struggling to climb the bank, Poonguzhali Ponmambadan, 61, unwrapped her sari dress and gave it to her husband to use as a rope.
“He used it as a harness to lift several old people,” she said.
More died than were rescued: Dam worker
Workers rescued from dam projects along the Trishuli valley described a disaster that unfolded with terrifying speed.
“There were at least 400 workers at the site,” Dev Shrestha, who was airlifted from the site where he was working, told AFP after his rescue. “More people died than were rescued.”
Worker Buddha Tamang said he survived only because he was inside a tunnel at the dam where he worked when the flood struck -- but he had managed to get out and reach help.
“I survived as I was in the tunnel,” said Tamang, who was airlifted on Thursday after being marooned for more than 24 hours.
“The senior officers working on the other side, they were all swept away.”
Another worker, Arjun Kumar Tamang, spoke of “massive damage” at the hydropower site where he had been.
“I don’t know how many people died but the force of the water swept everything away,” he said.
“I was at the powerhouse. I heard a loud noise. There was some seepage and we were told to come out,” said Ananay Sharma a 29-year-old engineer from India working on a project in the area.
“When I came out, everything was gone, only the river remained,” he added. “One residential camp completely washed away, another remains where we took shelter.”
Gorakh Khatka, an engineer who had been in the Shanti Bazar area near the epicenter of the disaster, ran for his life.
“All we got to react was 20 seconds before mud and water was as high as 20 feet (six meters) in the inundated area,” he said.
“We ran for our lives and spent more than 48 hours on a hill before help finally arrived.”

item.title: US judge rules Pentagon’s blacklisting of Anthropic unlawful
item.description:
A United States federal judge has ruled in favor of the artificial intelligence (AI) company Anthropic in its dispute with the Pentagon over its labeling as a “supply chain risk.”
California district judge Rita Lin concluded that the label constituted an attempt by the government to make an example of Anthropic after the company refused to allow unrestricted military use of its technology and criticized the Department of Defense’s use of AI.
Lin wrote in a 59-page ruling that “the empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics.”
She said the government’s actions were “based on a desire to make a public example out of Anthropic for its ‘arrogance’ in criticizing the government, not based on any articulable basis to believe that Anthropic would actually sabotage its model.”
An Anthropic spokesperson said they welcomed the judge’s ruling, saying in a statement: “We remain focused on working productively with the government to harness AI for our national security so all Americans benefit from this technology.”
The dispute between the San Francisco-based firm and the government broke out in February when President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth accused Anthropic of endangering national security after the company declined to allow unrestricted military use of its technology.
“We will not knowingly provide a product that puts America’s warfighters and civilians at risk,” wrote CEO Dario Amodei in a blog post back in February, adding that AI wasn’t reliable enough to be used in fully autonomous weapons systems and expressing concerns over mass surveillance.
In March, the Pentagon designated Anthropic a “supply chain risk” – a highly unusual label to apply to a US firm. The company complained of an “unlawful campaign of retaliation,” pointing out that the designation would have negative consequences for its business beyond defense deals.
Indeed, President Trump ordered all US government agencies to stop using Anthropic technology, calling it “a radical left, woke company” and “out-of-control” in a social media rant.
Defense Secretary Hegseth said companies would be expected to cut business links to Anthropic if they wanted to be considered for defense sector deals.
Shortly afterwards, OpenAI, Anthropic’s primary tech industry rival and operator of ChatGPT, made its own deal to work with the Pentagon.
In her ruling, Judge Lin, an appointee of former President Joe Biden, wrote that neither the US Constitution nor the federal statute the government invoked allows them to “impose sweeping penalties based principally on Anthropic’s critique of the Administration’s views.”
Earlier in the legal proceedings, Lin had temporarily blocked the Pentagon from labeling the company as a supply chain risk and blocked enforcement of Trump’s social media directive ordering all federal agencies to stop using Anthropic and its chatbot Claude.
In a preliminary hearing on July 30, Lin had said that the government’s position was “really troubling” and seemed “at odds to me with the First Amendment.”
The White House is yet to comment on the decision.
In the coming weeks, Anthropic is expected to launch on the US stock market with an initial public offering (IPO) that could potentially eclipse SpaceX’s record Wall Street debut in June, which raised $86 billion.

item.title: King Harald, ‘symbol’ of Norway, dead at 89
item.description:
Norway’s King Harald has died aged 89, the palace said on Friday, his 53-year-old son Crown Prince Haakon automatically succeeding him on the throne.
Haakon takes over a monarchy long hailed for its modernity and modesty, but beset by a string of scandals in recent years.
“It is with deep sadness that we announce that His Majesty King Harald passed away today. King Harald passed away peacefully at Oslo University Hospital on Friday, August 28 at 6:35am,” (0435 GMT) it said in a statement.
The flag at the royal palace in Oslo was lowered to half-mast, as crowds gathered outside the palace to pay their respects.
Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said he had received the news with “deep sorrow.”
“An entire nation mourns, and at the same time remains profoundly grateful for a long life devoted to Norway,” he said in a statement.
“King Harald loved Norway. And Norway loved its king.”
The government later announced a period of national mourning until the king was buried.
Hundreds of flowers had already been laid outside the palace the day before, after it announced the king was in “extremely serious” condition in hospital.
Vigdis Haug, 65, said she valued Harald’s ability to unify people.
“I think he has been such a down-to-earth king who has cared about all of us, and the words he always uses when he gives a speech are so wise and so valuable,” she told AFP.
Haug and others to whom AFP spoke pointed in particular to Harald’s speech after the neo-Nazi Anders Behring Breivik killed 77 people in twin attacks on July 22, 2011, in Norway’s worst massacre since World War II.
“He was someone who always seemed to find the words that brought us together and gave us a sense of security,” Caroline Vagle, a reporter for magazine Se og Hor, told AFP.
Neighboring Sweden’s King Carl XVI Gustaf called him “an outstanding representative of his country. He gave ‘All for Norway,’” referring to Harald’s royal motto.
Denmark’s King Frederik meanwhile called the late monarch “an extraordinary man.”
Britain’s King Charles III said he mourned the death of his “dear cousin,” hailing Harald as a “towering figure.”
Harald was king when the Oslo Accords between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) were negotiated in the 1990s, and Israeli President Isaac Herzog said he was “deeply saddened” by his passing.
Church bells were to ring across Norway at noon (1000 GMT) to mark the king’s passing.
Haakon was to meet with the government on Friday to formally inform it of the monarch’s death, and to announce the royal name and motto he has chosen.
After that, the flag over the royal palace will be raised to the top again, while another flag on the royal balcony and at other official buildings will remain at half-mast until after Harald’s funeral.
Haakon’s 22-year-old daughter Ingrid Alexandra also automatically becomes crown princess.
Europe’s oldest reigning monarch, King Harald had been in hospital in Oslo since August 17, suffering from haemolytic anaemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of red blood cells which leads to fatigue and shortness of breath.
Harald, who ascended the Norwegian throne in 1991, embodied an open and tolerant Norway during his reign.
He faced mounting health problems in his final years, forcing him to scale back his official schedule.
But he always ruled out abdicating, arguing that he took a lifelong oath before the Norwegian parliament.
The past year has been a turbulent one for the Norwegian royal family.
In addition to his own health struggles, his wife Queen Sonja, also 89, was briefly admitted to hospital in May due to heart problems.
Haakon’s wife Mette-Marit is under scrutiny for her ties to the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Documents published in January in the United States revealed her sustained and at times intimate correspondence with Epstein between 2011 and 2014, at a time when the American financier had already been convicted.
In June, Mette-Marit’s son from a relationship prior to her marriage to Haakon, Marius Borg Hoiby, was sentenced to four years in prison for two rapes. He has appealed the verdict.
Suffering herself from a serious lung disease, Mette-Marit, 53, had to undergo a lung transplant in July.
The royals remain broadly popular with the Norwegian public, in large part to Harald’s unifying status and his unassuming, modest lifestyle.

item.title: KU admission tests set for Dec 17-18, KUET on Jan 8
item.description:
Khulna University (KU) will hold admission tests for first-year undergraduate (honors) courses for the 2026-27 academic year on December 17 and 18 next.
The decision was taken at a meeting of the university’s Central Admission Committee on Thursday, according to a notification signed by the university’s acting Registrar Prof Dr SM Mahbubur Rahman.
According to the notification, the admission tests for “C” and “D” units will be held on December 17.
The “C” unit covers disciplines under the Schools of Arts and Humanities, Social Sciences, Law, Education and Fine Arts.
The “D” unit includes disciplines under the School of Management and Business Administration.
The tests for “A” and “B” units will be held on December 18.
The “A” unit covers disciplines under the School of Science, Engineering and Technology, while the “B” unit includes disciplines under the School of Life Sciences.
Meanwhile, Khulna University of Engineering and Technology (KUET) will hold its first-year admission test for the 2026-27 academic year on January 8, 2027.
The test is for admission to BSc Engineering, BURP and B Arch programs.
To ease transportation and accommodation problems for students from different parts of the country, KUET has decided to hold the admission test at centers in three divisional cities – Khulna, Dhaka and Rajshahi.
The decision was taken following discussions on undergraduate admissions at the 118th special meeting of KUET’s Academic Council held on Thursday, university sources said.
The admission test will be held under the multiple-choice question (MCQ) system.
An admission test committee has already been formed to ensure the smooth conduct of the examination, the sources added.

item.title: Murgh Afghani: A creamy, smoky chicken recipe to try at home
item.description:
If you are tired of preparing chicken the same way every time, Murgh Afghani can bring a delicious change to your dinner table. The dish combines yogurt, cream, herbs, spices, and cashews with smoky grilled chicken.
Tahmina Zaman shared the recipe.
First, marinate the bone-in chicken with salt, lemon juice, ginger paste, garlic paste and chaat masala. Leave it for 15–20 minutes.
In a separate bowl, whisk together the yogurt, fresh cream, dried fenugreek leaves, black pepper, chaat masala and garam masala.
Blend the onion, coriander leaves, mint leaves, green chilies, and cashews into a smooth paste.
Add the yogurt mixture and the onion-herb paste to the chicken. Mix everything thoroughly and marinate the chicken for about one hour. If possible, marinate it for two–three hours for a deeper flavor.
Heat some ghee in a flat pan. Remove the chicken pieces from the marinade and pan-roast or grill them one by one.
Let the edges of the chicken char slightly. This smoky flavor is an important part of Murgh Afghani.
Heat a little butter and oil in a flat-bottomed pan. Add the remaining marinade and cook until the spices are well sautéed.
Add the grilled chicken pieces and a small amount of water. Cover and cook over low to medium heat for 12–15 minutes.
Once the gravy thickens and the oil begins to separate, turn off the heat and mix in about one tbsp of fresh cream.
For an extra smoky aroma, heat a small piece of charcoal with a clove and a little ghee in a small bowl.
Place the bowl in the middle of the chicken, cover the pan, and let the smoke infuse for about five minutes.
Remove the charcoal bowl and cover the chicken again for a few minutes.
Serve the Murgh Afghani hot with roti or naan.

item.title: Can too much chili powder harm your health
item.description:
Red chili powder is a common ingredient in South Asian cooking, adding color, flavor, and heat to curries, bhuna dishes, and other foods. Chili peppers contain capsaicin, the compound responsible for their spicy taste.
For most people, eating spicy food in moderate amounts is generally safe. However, consuming very large quantities of chili powder can cause discomfort and may worsen symptoms in people with certain digestive conditions.
Capsaicin can stimulate receptors in the digestive tract. In some people, particularly those who are not accustomed to spicy food, eating large amounts may cause stomach pain, burning, nausea or diarrhea.
People with sensitive stomachs may notice these symptoms more frequently.
Spicy foods may trigger or aggravate heartburn and acid reflux in some people. Those who already experience gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) may therefore need to limit foods that consistently cause symptoms.
If you regularly experience burning in the chest or upper abdomen after eating spicy food, reducing your intake and discussing persistent symptoms with a doctor may be appropriate.
A common belief is that eating chili powder directly causes stomach ulcers. However, current evidence does
Stomach ulcers are commonly associated with factors such as Helicobacter pylori infection and the frequent not support this claim. use of certain painkillers. Spicy foods may exacerbate symptoms for someone who already has an ulcer, but they are not considered a primary cause of ulcers.
People with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) or other digestive sensitivities may find that spicy foods trigger abdominal pain, bloating or diarrhea.
If you notice that symptoms repeatedly appear after eating heavily spiced meals, reducing the amount of chili may help identify whether it is a personal trigger.
Spicy foods are not generally considered a direct cause of asthma. However, very spicy foods can cause coughing, irritation or other unpleasant sensations in some people. Anyone with asthma who notices symptoms after eating particular foods should discuss the pattern with a healthcare professional rather than assuming chili itself is the cause.
The quality of chili powder also matters. Poorly stored spices can become contaminated with molds, while some products may be adulterated with unauthorized substances. Buying spices from reliable sources and storing them properly can reduce these risks.
Avoiding chili completely is not necessary for most people. Chili peppers contain capsaicin and other plant compounds, and research has explored their potential antioxidant and other health effects. However, many claimed benefits of chili—such as preventing cancer or causing major weight loss—are not established in humans.
There is no single amount of chili powder that is considered excessive for everyone. Tolerance varies from person to person.
A practical approach is to use chili according to your tolerance and reduce the amount if it consistently causes heartburn, stomach pain, diarrhea, or other discomfort.

item.title: The last piece of identity
item.description:
Mayyu Ali was born in 1991 in Maungdaw Township, Myanmar's Rakhine State (Arakan), the youngest of six children in a fisherman's family.
He writes under the name Mayyu, taken from the mountains and river near his childhood home. His early poems appeared in magazines in Myanmar. In 2017, he was among some 700,000 Rohingya who crossed into Bangladesh after the military operations that began on 25 August.
Two years later he had a poetry collection in print, an online platform of his own, and readers in camps holding close to a million people.
The literature he was joining had barely been written down. Rohingya is largely an oral language and, until recently, was rarely committed to paper.
It has also had little institutional footing.
A Rohingya-language program began on the Burma Broadcasting Service in August 1961; it was closed at the end of October 1965, on the same day as programs in Lahu and Pa-O.
The songs remain hard to find on paper. Documenting the tarana, a Rohingya song genre, the researchers Kazi Fahmida Farzana, Peter Sammonds, and Bayes Ahmed worked with Rohingya refugees in Malaysia.
They assembled their archive from the few lyrics that had been written down, from transcribing singers, and from recordings community members had made themselves.
Mayyu Ali. Photo: Collected
Their chapter appeared in Religious Sounds Beyond the Global North from Amsterdam University Press in 2024.
Before any of the anthologies, Ali printed The Blossom, a selection of his early poems, and distributed it around the camps.
In April 2019, two poets arrived from outside: the British poet James Byrne and the Bangladeshi-French poet Shehzar Doja.
Over two days they worked with twenty refugees in what they were told were the first creative writing workshops held in the camps. Ali had helped set them up.
He could not attend.
After the sessions, the editors asked participants to send work. The poems came in faster than they could be read—ten or more on some days. Few of the poets had pens or paper; almost all had mobile phones.
A planned pamphlet of about forty pages turned into a book.
I am a Rohingya: Poetry from the Camps and Beyond, published by Arc Publications in July 2019, ran to eighty-three pages: ten of the workshop poets, alongside Rohingya writers from the wider diaspora, poems in Burmese, three songs in Rohingya, and folk songs sung by Jani Alam. Many contributors used pseudonyms; being named would put them at risk.
The Poetry Book Society made it the inaugural title in its World Choice selection, chosen by the poet Ilya Kaminsky.
By then Ali had built something of his own.
In 2019 he and a group of friends launched Art Garden Rohingya, an online platform for Rohingya poetry and art—unfunded, with no institution behind it, run from inside the camps.
By 2022 it had gathered work by more than a hundred Rohingya poets, writers, and artists.
It has mattered particularly to women with few other routes into print. Shahida Win published her first poem there in 2019: "Thami Maha," Daughter the Great. She has said she wrote it after speaking with Rohingya women and girls about the discrimination they faced.
In 2020 she was selected by UNHCR as a youth leader and traveled to Geneva to speak on behalf of her community; in January 2023, she was invited to present her work at the Dhaka Lit Fest.
Others followed. The photographer Sahat Zia Hero founded Rohingyatographer in 2021, with support from the creative producer David Palazón.
The collective publishes a magazine and photobooks, among them Unseen Courage, curated in 2023 by Ishrat Bibi—the first monograph of work by ten Rohingya women photographers.
In 2024, it supported the historian Aman Ullah in publishing A History of Rohingyas to 1948. Separately, the Rohingya Cultural Memory Center in Cox's Bazar, an initiative of the International Organization for Migration, has identified at least twenty-three genres of Rohingya folk music, along with dozens of futhi—fairy tales told through song—and sixty-four sewing techniques.
Ali's own books span the years before and after resettlement.
Exodus: Between Genocide and Me appeared in 2019, while he was still in the camps; The White Elephant, an illustrated story told through the eyes of a Rohingya boy, followed.
He was resettled in Canada in 2021 and completed a master's degree at the University of Waterloo in 2024. His memoir, written with the French journalist Émilie Lopes, was published in French by Grasset in 2022 as L'effacement and in English in 2025 as Eradication, translated by Siba Barkataki.
The memoir makes one decision that repays attention: it does not begin with the burning. Reviewers note that it opens instead on the Purma River, on bamboo forests and morning mist over the Mayu Mountains, and on a boy learning the Burmese alphabet in classrooms shared with Rakhine and Hindu children. Belonging first, rupture afterwards.
He is not the only one writing from exile. Habiburahman, who reached Australia by boat in December 2009 and spent thirty-two months in detention before his release, remains stateless; he wrote First, They Erased Our Name with Sophie Ansel.
Ali now directs a Rohingya language preservation project at the Community Rebuilding Centre, transcribing oral traditions into Rohingya script with Burmese and English translations.
Four collections are complete. As the ninth anniversary of the exodus approaches on 25 August, the writing that might hold the language is being done in Ukhiya and Teknaf—and in the cities its authors have scattered to.
Ehatasham Ul Hoque Eiten teaches English at Daffodil International University, Dhaka, and writes on migration, identity, politics, literature, and education in South Asia.

item.title: In shadow of Premier League, Serie A flexes financial muscle
item.description:
For Italian football this has been a chastening year, yet, ahead of a likely frenzy before their transfer window shuts on September 1, Serie A clubs have spent the summer asserting their place in Europe's financial pecking order.
In both overall outlay and net spend, Serie A is a clear second among the 'Big Five' leagues.
While fee structures, conditional payments and financial sleights-of-hand can make the precise transfer values a little hazy, German site Transfermarkt on Thursday put Italy's total outgoings at more than one billion euros ($1.165bn), far ahead of La Liga, at three-quarters-of-a-billion, and then the Bundesliga.
In all, the 20 Serie A clubs are almost 430mn euros in the red this summer, against just under 300mn euros in Spain. Both the Bundesliga and French Ligue 1 are in profit.
Of course, the 'Big Five' is a misleading phrase. European club football has become the Premier League and everyone else. English clubs have, so far, spent 3.2bn euros, more than the other four league put together.
The second round of the Serie A season opens Friday with AC Milan, for now restored to their role as Italy's biggest spenders, hosting smartly-dressed yoyo club Venezia.
When Milan spent a reported 74mn euros to acquire Goncalo Ramos from Paris Saint-Germain, he became the most expensive Serie A signing since Juventus bought Dusan Vlahovic from Fiorentina five years earlier.
With Diego Moreira, coming from Strasbourg for 50mn euros, Milan have spent a total of almost 160mn euros, a whisker more than Juventus, with plenty of moves to come.
Under new boss Ruben Amorim, Milan opened the season with a 2-1 win at Torino.
On Thursday, Amorim did not rule out further recruits.
"We have to wait five more days until the transfer window closes," the Portuguese coach, who started last season in the Premier League with Manchester United, told his pre-match press conference.
"If someone arrives, it will be because they can help us both now and in the future."
He made clear that the transfer market was not simply about spending to bring players in.
"It's impossible to train during the week with 27 players. Nobody is going to be prepared, nobody is going to be satisfied, so there are some players that if they stay, they will not be part of the squad," he said, when asked about reports that the club was trying to unload Fikayo Tomori, Youssouf Fofana and Santiago Gimenez.
After a summer in which Italy missed the World Cup, sparking a debate on the lack of talent in the national team, Amorim said clubs need to develope from within.
"We need to take time and believe in our young players," he said. "We are going to have some problems with young players in some games, but big surprises happen.
"Everyone wants everything really fast and I'm a little bit old school. I think a lot of things will take time."
Yet on the opening weekend, five of the six biggest spenders, Milan, champions Inter Milan, Juventus, Roma and Napoli all won. The exception were Fiorentina, trying to spend their way into the top end of the table, who crashed to Roma.

item.title: Arteta braced for 'tough' Martinelli, Jesus exits from Arsenal
item.description:
Mikel Arteta revealed he has had difficult conversations with forwards Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus as both Brazilian internationals appear set to depart Arsenal.
"It's inevitable, at some point you need to have certain discussions and say certain things that sometimes are tough," said Arteta. Martinelli left training early on Thursday amid speculation he is set for a move to Saudi side Al Hilal for a fee that could reportedly rise to œ50million ($68 million).
"I think everybody knows and recognises how much we love Gabi (Martinelli). Whatever the outcome is, it will be because everybody agrees to that," added Arteta. Jesus has fallen well down the pecking order during an injury disrupted time in north London and was not even included in training on Thursday as he enters the final 12 months of his contract.
"It's something to do with the numbers that we have in the squad at the moment and the way we're managing that kind of situation individually with all the players -- they have some personal situations," Arteta said of the former Manchester City striker.
Arsenal have been linked with bolstering their forward line with a move for Atletico Madrid's Julian Alvarez. The Argentine is caught in an acrimonious stand-off after Atletico refused to let him depart the Spanish capital for Barcelona.
"Don't go there," said Arteta about Arsenal's interest in Alvarez. "I'm not going to make any comment about any player that is not with us." Ezri Konsa is already an Arsenal player and could make his debut back at Villa Park on Monday after securing a œ51 million move from Aston Villa.
The England international could receive a frosty reception but Arteta said that would not influence his decision in throwing Konsa into action.
"If I see something different in the player then I may have a question about that, but the way I've seen Ezri since day one, knowing his personality really well and through people that have worked with him, I have no concern there."
Bruno Guimaraes could also be fit to make his first competitive Arsenal appearance after missing the 3-0 win over Coventry last weekend due to a groin problem.

item.title: Welbeck scores first Chelsea goal in League Cup win over Luton
item.description:
Danny Welbeck netted his first Chelsea goal as the Blues shrugged aside third-tier Luton 2-0 at Stamford Bridge to reach the League Cup third round.
