The front three of Joao Pedro, Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers caught the eye in a 3-2 win at Fulham on Monday to open the Xabi Alonso era at Chelsea with victory.
But 35-year-old Welbeck showed he will be a useful addition to the Chelsea squad by heading in Malo Gusto's cross to break Luton's resistence after a goalless first half.
"I bring the average age a little bit higher!" Welbeck said on what he brings to a Chelsea squad that has lacked experience in recent seasons.
"The experience of playing games, being around loads of different dressing rooms and knowing what is a good dressing room and a bad one. Knowing what it takes to achieve something special."
Hakeem Odoffin's own goal killed the tie off after another dangerous delivery by Estevao as Chelsea set up a home tie against Leeds in the last 32.
Mike Penders started in goal for Chelsea after Robert Sanchez's error-strewn display against Fulham.
And Alonso may soon have the experience of Emi Martinez to count on with a deal to bring the Argentina international to London from Aston Villa reportedly close to completion.
But Martinez's international teammate Enzo Fernandez was not involved as he appears set for a move to Manchester City.
"We want to have a complete squad in all aspects. In quality, personality, young and experienced players -- so the young players get help, that they are still players to develop," said Alonso.
"I'm happy with the energy and attitude of the players."
Fulham also booked their place in round three with a 3-0 win over AFC Wimbledon.
First-half goals from Emile Smith Rowe and Rodrigo Muniz put Alvaro Arbeloa's side in command before Gonzalo Garcia came off the bench to net for the second time in two games since his move from Real Madrid.
Fulham travel to West Ham in round three.

item.title: Messi's Inter Miami appoint Gonzalez as new head coach
item.description:
Lionel Messi's Inter Miami on Thursday appointed his fellow Argentine Cristian "Kily" Gonzalez as new head coach of the reigning Major League Soccer champions.
Gonzalez, who hails from superstar Messi's hometown Rosario, will attempt to turn around Miami's poor run of post-World Cup form under interim manager Guillermo Hoyos.
"Inter Miami CF announced today that it has reached an agreement with Cristian Alberto 'Kily' Gonzalez to become the Club's new First Team head coach," said a club statement.
Hoyos will remain in post until his replacement's US work permit is approved, it added.
Gonzalez, 52, played left wing for European giants Inter Milan, Valencia and Zaragoza in a career that also included 56 international caps for Argentina between 1995-2005.
He moved into management in 2020, taking the helm at three Argentine club sides before his move to Miami.
The MLS Cup holders have endured a rough spell since the North American league's mid-season World Cup break, despite adding Brazil's Casemiro from Manchester United to a star-packed squad.
The side under Hoyos has lost four of its last five games, remaining second in the Eastern Conference but slipping 10 points adrift of leaders Nashville.
Hoyos on Thursday received a one-game ban and fine for the club's multiple violations of the league's late kick-off policy, his team repeatedly slow to return to the field after half-time breaks.
Hoyos, previously Miami's sporting director and a longtime friend of club captain and talisman Messi, only stepped into the temporary role in April after Javier Mascherano departed the club for "personal reasons."
"Inter Miami would like to especially highlight and thank Hoyos for his commitment and full dedication to the Club, demonstrated by his willingness to assume the role during this period, which began last April," said the club statement.

item.title: Raphinha, Lopez strike again as Barca beat Athletic
item.description:
Raphinha and Fermin Lopez goals helped Spanish champions Barcelona beat Athletic Bilbao 2-0 on Thursday in La Liga to continue their perfect start to the season.
The Catalan giants eased to a solid victory over their Basque visitors in their first game of the season at the partially-rebuilt Camp Nou, with new arrival Rodri coming on for his Barca debut.
Raphinha rounded the goalkeeper and slid home in the 37th minute to give Barca the lead, and Lopez netted after 82 minutes to secure the points, with the Catalans missing several chances for more goals and twice hitting the woodwork.
"Very happy to play my first game, happy with the victory, we've got two from two," Rodri told DAZN. "It's important to keep building up rhythm and adapting to this great team. My first minutes and (I had some) good feelings."
Barca coach Hansi Flick made three changes to the team that thrashed Elche 5-0 last weekend, handing Anthony Gordon his first start for the club, while bringing Pedri Gonzalez into midfield and picking Pau Cubarsi in defence.
The German kept Raphinha playing up front as a makeshift number nine, after the departures of Robert Lewandowski and Ferran Torres. Barca have fruitlessly tried to pry Julian Alvarez away from Atletico Madrid, who will not negotiate with the Spanish champions for the Argentina forward.
However, Raphinha netted twice from his striker's role against Elche and was on target again for Barca at Camp Nou, giving them a deserved lead at half-time. "It doesn't matter which position Rapha plays, as a captain he's shown total commitment to this team, to this club," Flick told reporters.
"You can see the supporters are connected with him and it's really good."
The Brazilian nodded against the post from Xavi Espart's cross midway through the first half and Lamine Yamal's follow-up effort was deflected wide, with Barca controlling the game. Eventually, they took the lead when Pedri slipped Raphinha through on goal, with the Brazilian rounding Unai Simon and rolling home.
Teenage star Yamal should have doubled Barca's lead before the interval but Simon made a fine save to deny him, while Gordon complained that he would have had an open goal if the Spain international had knocked the ball across to him. Gordon arrowed a shot narrowly over early in the second half as Barcelona probed for a second goal.
Yamal, still not at his best level since suffering a hamstring injury in April, hit the crossbar with an effort from the edge of the box. Simon saved twice from Lopez, who netted a brace in the opener. Flick sent on former Manchester City midfielder Rodri for his debut in midfield, leaving 10 Spaniards and Gordon on the pitch for Barca.
- Securing the points -
The champions were in the ascendency but Athletic threatened on a rare venture forward, with Oihan Sancet drilling against the post. Barcelona eventually found their second after a mistake from Athletic defender Aymeric Laporte, clumsily nudging Barca substitute Karim Adeyemi's cross past Simon, for Lopez to tuck into an empty net.
Adeyemi should have netted a third late on when Yamal picked him out at the back post but Simon denied the German from point-blank range. Yamal's second half performance was an improvement on a disappointing opening 45 minutes and his struggles against Elche, and Rodri said that the forward is improving.
"Maybe Lamine came from a moment where he was a bit down and today we tried to help him get back up and saw his best version, even though he didn't score," added Rodri, Spain's World Cup winning captain.
"The goals will come because the talent is there."
Athletic Bilbao have started their season with two defeats under new coach Edin Terzic. "I'm not a constant winner, I'm a constant trier," said former Borussia Dortmund coach Terzic.
"I'm fully of belief and trust when I see how we worked in these two games and in the training ground, sooner or later we'll get what we deserve and turn results in our favour."

item.title: Asha Bhosle's last film song set for September release
item.description:
The last film song recorded by singer Asha Bhosle, "Ae Meri Zindagi, Tu Chupi Hai Kahan," is scheduled for release on September 8, the makers of Om Ka Hari said.
Bhosle recorded the track in late 2023, when she was in her 90s. The film, directed by Harish Vyas, is a drama-comedy centered on a father-son relationship. Its cast includes Anshuman Jha, Raghubir Yadav, Soni Razdan, and Ayesha Kapur.
According to the makers, the release date was chosen deliberately, as it coincides with what would have been Bhosle's birthday.
Vyas said the timing was meant to honor the singer's body of work and its effect on listeners across generations.
Jha, who appears in the film, said the song holds a personal meaning for him, tied to the film's theme of a son expressing feelings toward his father that he never voiced in real life.
Bhosle died on April 12 this year at age 92. The cause was multi-organ failure, and she was being treated at Breach Candy Hospital in Mumbai at the time. Over a career of more than 70 years, she recorded upward of 12,000 songs and became known for tracks such as "Dum Maro Dum," "Piya Tu Ab To Aaja," "Chura Liya Hai Tumne Jo Dil Ko," and "Yeh Mera Dil."
A release date for the film itself has not been finalized.

item.title: Study of 4,500 animals reveals how human presence changes wildlife behaviour
item.description:
Wildlife may respond to the physical presence of people far more than scientists previously understood, according to a new study that tracked more than 4,500 animals across the United States.
Researchers from the University of California, Santa Barbara, the Smithsonian’s National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute, and Yale University combined GPS data from 37 animal species with anonymised cellphone location data.
The study, published in the journal Science, found that animals respond differently to human activity depending on the species and how much the surrounding landscape has already been altered by people.
The findings could help scientists develop more effective, species-specific approaches to wildlife conservation.
“Humans have complicated effects on wildlife — from our physical presence to how we reshape habitats,” said Ruth Oliver, an assistant professor at UCSB’s Bren School of Environmental Science & Management and co-lead author of the study.
The researchers took advantage of COVID-19 lockdowns, when restrictions sharply changed people’s movements. This created a rare opportunity to examine the effects of human presence separately from long-term changes to the environment.
The team studied weekly GPS records of 4,581 individual mammals and birds during comparable periods in 2019 and 2020.
To measure human movement, the researchers used anonymised cellphone location data with neighbourhood-level detail. According to the researchers, this was the first study to use such data to examine how people’s physical presence affects animal movement.
Scott Yanco, a research ecologist at the Smithsonian’s National Zoo and another co-lead author, said the cellphone data provided a rare opportunity to measure the direct effects of human presence on wildlife.
The study found that 57% of the species examined were affected by both human presence and changes to the landscape. Human presence was associated with changes in the territory or environmental niche of 67% of mammal species and 68% of bird species.
About 67% of mammal species and 41% of bird species reduced the amount of habitat they used when faced with a combination of human presence and landscape changes.
Animals were particularly sensitive to people in areas with relatively little development, such as national parks, compared with heavily developed cities.
However, wildlife did not respond in the same way.
Wolves, for example, expanded their habitat use in response to human presence, possibly because they tend to move farther away from people or spread out to avoid human activity.
White-tailed deer showed a different pattern. Their environmental niche expanded as landscapes became more developed but became smaller as human presence increased. Sandhill cranes showed the opposite response.
Oliver said the findings highlight the importance of developing conservation measures for individual species because animals have different habitat needs, behaviours and threats.
The research is part of the COVID-19 Bio-Logging Initiative, an international project that examined how wildlife responded to the sharp drop in human activity during pandemic lockdowns, a period researchers described as the “anthropause”.
The wider initiative involved about 600 researchers and partners and collected around 1 billion location records from nearly 13,000 animals.
The researchers said combining animal GPS tracking with human movement data can help distinguish between the effects of infrastructure and the effects of people simply being present.
They are now investigating whether changes in animal behaviour caused by human activity and climate change help wildlife adapt or instead indicate stress that could increase their risk of death.
Oliver said the findings offer hope that better policies could help humans and wildlife coexist by identifying where and when animals need more space.

item.title: Five-year-old child killed in Rohingya camp gunfight
item.description:
A five-year-old child was killed in a gunfight between armed groups at the Kutupalong Rohingya camp in Ukhiya, Cox’s Bazar, on Thursday evening.
The child, identified as Mojahed, sustained a gunshot wound to the head during the firing. His mother Tahera Begum and 6 others were also injured.
The gunfight took place around the B-40 and B-41 blocks of Camp-8 East at Kutupalong.
Police initially suspect that the gunfight took place between members of the Arakan Rohingya Army (ARA) and the Rohingya Solidarity Organization (RSO).
Police Superintendent Asaduzzaman, deputy commander of the 8-Armed Police Battalion (APBn) assigned to Ukhiya, disclosed the incident on Friday morning.
Police and local sources said gunfire suddenly began in the camp on Thursday evening. More than 100 gunshots were heard, prompting many people to leave their homes and seek shelter.
Mojahed, son of Nur Alam, a resident of Camp-8 East, was rescued in critical condition and taken to Cox’s Bazar District Sadar Hospital. He died while undergoing treatment.
Among the seven injured, three were women, including Mojahed’s mother. Some of the injured were transferred from Cox’s Bazar Sadar Hospital to Chittagong Medical College Hospital for advanced treatment.
A drive is underway to identify and arrest those involved in the incident.

item.title: Saudi fire victim returns home after eight years, buried in Rajshahi
item.description:
Shyamal Uddin Majhi, who was killed in a fire at a sofa manufacturing factory in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, was buried beside his parents at his family graveyard in Bagmara, Rajshahi, at 11am on Friday.
His body reached his home in Dangapara village of Marugram under Jhikra Union of Bagmara upazila at around 3am on Friday.
The bodies of Shyamal and 9 other Bangladeshis arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport on a Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight at around 4pm on Thursday. The bodies were then handed over to the relatives of the deceased.
Shyamal was a resident of Marugram under Jhikra Union of Bagmara upazila in Rajshahi district. His son-in-law Mizanur Rahman went to the airport to receive his body.
Mizanur said Shyamal’s namaz-e-janaza was held at 11am on Friday, with relatives and local residents attending. He was later buried beside his parents at the family graveyard.
Shyamal had gone to Saudi Arabia around 8 years ago in the hope of improving his family’s financial condition. He worked at a sofa manufacturing factory in the Manfuhah area of Riyadh.
On the night of August 9, a fire broke out at the factory, killing 16 Bangladeshi workers, including Shyamal.
Family members had been waiting for Shyamal to return home after 8 years. According to family sources, he had been preparing to return and had told them during their last conversation that he would return home soon.
His wife and 3 daughters had been waiting for him. His death has left the family facing uncertainty, as he was the family’s only earning member.
Local residents have called on the government, elected representatives, affluent individuals and those involved in expatriate welfare to stand beside the bereaved family.
Bagmara Upazila Nirbahi Officer Selim Ahmed said: “After hearing about the death, the upazila administration provided Tk 25,000 and dry food. They also received Tk 35,000 at the airport. Since the deceased has 3 daughters, I have asked prominent people in the area to look after them. As they are studying, we will support them.”

Ministers’ responsibility for coordination in districts, or a new authority?
item.description:
The government has once again divided responsibility for the country’s 64 districts among ministers, state ministers, and Whips of the Jatiya Sangsad (national parliament).

According to the government, those designated will supervise and co-ordinate law and order, crime and narcotics control, corruption prevention, good governance, transparency, accountability, and official development and public welfare activities.

However, in the past, similar arrangements drew allegations of undermining the authority of local members of parliament (MPs) and creating dual authority over the administration.

This time, the phrasing outlining these duties is somewhat different. The appointees have not been granted direct executive powers. Instead, they have been tasked with supervision and co-ordination without curtailing the statutory powers of local government institutions and other constitutional and statutory bodies.

Yet the question remains: will this remain limited to mere oversight or co-ordination, or will it translate into political control and the exercise of power?

Furthermore, in districts where the ruling party has no MP, what will their relationship be with opposition members? THere are also questions over whether the local administration will face impediments in discharging its duties.

The practice of assigning specific districts to ministers, state ministers, and Whips has precedence. The Sheikh Hasina-led government introduced a similar arrangement between 1996 and 2001. Subsequently, the BNP government implemented a comparable measure in 2001.

Last Thursday, the Cabinet Division distributed responsibility for the 64 districts among 30 ministers, state ministers, and three parliamentary Whips. Some have been assigned one district, while others have been given responsibility for two to three.

The official notification stated that during the previous fascist regime, although development allocations existed on paper, widespread corruption led to systemic looting. A portion of the looted funds was laundered abroad, while the remainder was used in ways detrimental to public and state security, including narcotics and social degradation.

In this context, the notification said, these responsibilities have been assigned to ensure law and order, curb corruption and drug abuse, and guarantee good governance at the district level.

Legal and political questions

The notification regarding district duties notes that this decision was taken in accordance with Article 55(2) of the Constitution and relevant provisions of the Rules of Business.

Political analysts believe there are considerations beyond legal and political questions. For instance, several ministries are currently dealing with crisis situations.

Article 55(2) of the Constitution states: "The executive authority of the Republic shall, in accordance with this Constitution, be exercised by or on the authority of the Prime Minister." That is to say, the primary political authority over the executive or administrative power of the State resides with the Prime Minister. Under his authority, ministers, ministries, and public authorities exercise these powers.

According to the notification, the designated individuals will offer necessary counsel to district government offices to maintain law and order, control drug abuse and illicit trafficking, prevent smuggling, and curb legacy crime.

They also will oversee various development and public welfare activities, including the implementation of the government’s electoral manifesto, poverty alleviation, employment generation, and social security. If necessary, they may also attend district-level meetings to provide advice.

Hamidur Rahman Azad, Assistant Secretary General of Bangladesh Jamaat-e-IslamiPast experience is far from positive. This could turn into a mechanism to hold local elected representatives hostage. Under the guise of development oversight, opportunities will arise to encroach upon the rights of others. This will create friction not only with opposition representatives but with those of the ruling party as well.

The question remains: how much power will a minister exercise upon receiving responsibility for a district, and to what extent will they observe the limits of oversight?

Political analysts believe there are considerations beyond legal and political questions. For instance, several ministries are currently dealing with crisis situations. Ministers heading these ministries may find their core ministerial work disrupted while attending to district duties.

Hamidur Rahman Azad, Assistant Secretary General of Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami, told Prothom Alo, "Past experience is far from positive. This could turn into a mechanism to hold local elected representatives hostage. Under the guise of development oversight, opportunities will arise to encroach upon the rights of others. This will create friction not only with opposition representatives but with those of the ruling party as well."

What does past experience show?

The practice of assigning specific districts to ministers, state ministers, and Whips has precedence. The Sheikh Hasina-led government introduced a similar arrangement between 1996 and 2001. Subsequently, the BNP government implemented a comparable measure in 2001.

However, in 2001, the BNP-led Four-Party Alliance government did not assign any districts to the two ministers from Jamaat-e-Islami. All 64 districts were allocated among BNP ministers and state ministers.

At that time, most ministers were assigned their home districts. M. Saifur Rahman, the then Finance and Planning Minister, was given responsibility for Sylhet and Moulvibazar. His home was in Moulvibazar, and he served as the MP for Sylhet-1.

Abdul Mannan Bhuiyan, the then BNP Secretary General and Local Government Minister, was assigned his home district of Narsingdi. In districts with multiple ministers or state ministers, some were given charge of neighbouring districts.

In the current allocation, cabinet members have not been assigned their home districts; instead, some have received one or more neighbouring districts.

Badiul Alam Majumdar, Secretary of Citizens for Good GovernanceNo benefits were reaped from this practice in the past, nor does it have any legal foundation. Instead, local government institutions should be strengthened. Rather than doing so, the government is paralysing local government by appointing administrators.

In 2003, Anwar Hossain Manju, Chairman of the Jatiya Party (JP) and MP for Pirojpur, challenged this mechanism in the High Court. In 2006, the High Court declared the arrangement illegal and unconstitutional.

During the court hearings, arguments were raised regarding the potential conflict between a minister's political and administrative authority and the jurisdiction of locally elected MPs. It was argued that interference from the designated minister prevented local administrations from working independently and restricted the ability of local MPs to contribute to development efforts.

Beyond ministers and state ministers, secretaries have also historically been given district-level responsibilities. In April 2021, to coordinate Covid-19 response and relief efforts for affected populations, 64 senior secretaries, secretaries, and officers of equivalent rank were assigned one district each. Several MPs from the then-ruling Awami League and opposition Jatiya Party opposed the move in Parliament.

Hence, the crucial question remains how the government intends to avoid the very risks previously viewed as undermining local MPs and creating dual authority over the administration.

In districts with one or more ministers, state ministers, and MPs, defining the exact boundaries of power between them and the newly assigned minister will also be critical.

What happens in opposition-held districts?

An analysis of the 13th Parliamentary Election results shows that the BNP failed to win a single seat across eight districts: Kurigram, Nilphamari, Gaibandha, Rangpur, Chapainawabganj, Meherpur, Satkhira, and Chuadanga. Together, these districts account for 30 seats.

In six of these districts, candidates from Jamaat-e-Islami secured victory in every seat. In Kurigram and Rangpur, Jamaat’s ally, the National Citizen Party (NCP), won one seat each, while Jamaat secured all remaining seats.

In Parliament, ruling and opposition parties are exchanging heated exchanges over various issues. On several fronts, opposition parties are also taking to the field with street programmes, including long marches. In such a context, assigning BNP ministers, state ministers, and Whips to Jamaat and opposition-dominated districts raises concerns over whether new conflicts will emerge.

Recently in Kushtia, clashes erupted between Jamaat MP Amir Hamza and activists from Gono Odhikar Parishad, an ally of the BNP, leading to filing cases and counter-cases. State Minister for Power, Aninda Islam Amit, has been assigned responsibility for Meherpur, Kushtia, and Jhenaidah districts. Notably, both parliamentary seats in Meherpur are held by Jamaat.

Social Welfare Minister AZM Zahid Hossain has been assigned Lalmonirhat, Panchagarh, and Nilphamari districts. Cultural Affairs Minister Nitai Roy Chowdhury has been given charge of Chuadanga. All MPs in Nilphamari and Chuadanga belong to Jamaat. How they will receive these two BNP ministers remains to be seen.

Law Minister Asaduzzaman has been given responsibility for Satkhira, Khulna, and Bagerhat. State Minister for Public Administration Abdul Bari has been assigned Bogura and Chapainawabganj. State Minister for Local Government Mir Shahe Alam is in charge of Rangpur, Gaibandha, and Kurigram. Jamaat-e-Islami holds a strong organisational presence in these districts.

Badiul Alam Majumdar, Secretary of Citizens for Good Governance (SHUJAN), who writes on constitutional matters, told Prothom Alo regarding the government’s move: “Whatever title is used, assigned ministers and state ministers will attempt to act as the overlords of those districts.”

According to him, where there are ministers or MPs more influential than them, conflict will inevitably arise.

This was entirely unnecessary, he argued.

Pointing out that no benefits were reaped from this practice in the past, nor does it have any legal foundation, he further said, “Instead, local government institutions should be strengthened. Rather than doing so, the government is paralysing local government by appointing administrators.”

item.title: Poor people’s trains taken off the rails one after another
item.description:
At one time, six local and mail trains operated on the Bhairab–Mymensingh railway route. People could travel to distant markets, workplaces or homes by paying fares of Tk 10–20. During the coronavirus pandemic, four local trains and one mail train on the route were suspended. Only the Mymensingh Mail remained. It too has been suspended since last Monday (24 August).

The distance from Bhairab in Kishoreganj to Mymensingh is 116 kilometres. The fare on the route is Tk 40 for a local train and Tk 55 for a mail train.

As all the local and mail trains were suspended, only intercity trains are now operating on the route. The fare on these trains is Tk 127. They also do not stop at every station. As a result, poor and low-income people on this railway route have lost the opportunity to travel at lower fares and now have to spend more to reach their destinations.

Bangladesh Railway says the Nasirabad train has been temporarily suspended due to an acute shortage of locomotives. The railway authorities, however, have no specific information on when the train will resume operations.

Ibrahimabad Station is located in Bhuapur upazila of Tangail, on the eastern bank of the Jamuna Bridge. The Mymensingh Mail, locally known as the Nasirabad Mail, operates from this station to Chattogram via the Bhairab–Mymensingh railway route.

The distance from Ibrahimabad to Chattogram is 631 kilometres. The train stops at 50 stations along the way. Its official travel time to the destination is 17 hours and 20 minutes. The train departs Ibrahimabad at 3:00 am and reaches Chattogram at 8:20 pm. In the opposite direction, it departs Chattogram at 4:15 pm and reaches Ibrahimabad Station at 9:00 am the following day.

According to railway sources, the Nasirabad train service was kept operational with three rakes, or sets of trains including engines and coaches. For about a month, the train was operated for two days and kept suspended for one day. Later, its operation was suspended without any written announcement.

The Bhairab–Mymensingh railway route is connected to several important railway routes in the country. Trains on the Dhaka–Kishoreganj route use this route. Trains to Chattogram also travel along the same route. Three intercity trains operate on the Dhaka–Kishoreganj route. The Bijoy Express intercity train operates between Jamalpur and Chattogram.

On 24 March 2020, four local trains operating on the Bhairab–Mymensingh route were suspended. The Isha Khan Mail (39/40) was also suspended on 12 March of the same year. The train, which operated from Mymensingh to Dhaka via Bhairab, was known as ‘ Goriber Train (Poor people’s train)’.

Low-fare trains suspended, costs on the rise

The distance from Ibrahimabad to Bhairab is 333 kilometres. The Nasirabad train stopped at 27 stations along this route. It has been learnt that passengers at these stations have been facing the greatest difficulties since the train was suspended. This is particularly the case at small stations where intercity trains do not stop. The minimum fare on local trains was Tk 5, while the minimum fare on mail trains was Tk 15. According to railway sources, the minimum fare on intercity trains is Tk 45.

Locals said local and mail trains were the main mode of transportation for poor and low-income people in the area. This railway route is an important means of communication for people in Mymensingh, Kishoreganj, Sherpur and Jamalpur.

According to them, a large section of the population in these areas is engaged in agriculture and local businesses for their livelihoods. Clothes, shoes, cosmetics, mats, paddy, milk, eggs, bananas, chickens, fruits, vegetables and various agricultural products are transported from one market to another. Low-fare local and mail trains played an important role in transporting these goods.

Locals said the cost of transporting these goods would increase following the suspension of the trains. At the same time, the transportation costs of ordinary people would also rise. This would affect the lives of people on the margins. The small, station-based economy would also come to a standstill.

Train was a lifeline for working people

Many people from greater Mymensingh work as labourers in Bhairab, Brahmanbaria, Sylhet, Cumilla and Chattogram. The Nasirabad train was their main means of transportation between their homes and workplaces. The train never faced a shortage of passengers.

At around 11:45 am last Wednesday, numerous working people were seen waiting for a train on Platform No. 2 of Bhairab Railway Station. Among them were Azizur Rahman, Murshid Mia, Aizuddin and Jewel Mia. All of them are from Purbadhala in Netrokona. They work as agricultural labourers in different villages in Cumilla. They return home once a month. They had returned home by the Nasirabad train a week earlier. On Wednesday, while returning to Cumilla, they went to Purbadhala Station and learned that the train had been suspended. They were forced to change vehicles several times and travel by road to Bhairab Railway Station. From there, they were waiting to travel to Cumilla by the Karnaphuli train.

Azizur Rahman said, “Before, I would board the train in Cumilla and get off at my home station (Purbadhala). It cost Tk 100. Today, it cost me nearly Tk 300 just to reach Bhairab. It will cost another Tk 60 to go to Cumilla.”

Calculating his expenses, Azizur said he paid Tk 10 for an auto-rickshaw from his home to Purbadhala. From there, he took a CNG-run auto-rickshaw to Shyamganj for Tk 40. He then travelled to Gouripur for another Tk 40 and to Khaltapara for Tk 15. He then paid Tk 150 for a bus to reach Bhairab. He spent another Tk 15 to reach the railway station. The train fare to Cumilla is Tk 60.

Before Azizur could finish speaking, another member of the group, Aizuddin, said they used to return home every month or every month and a half. Since the Nasirabad train was suspended, they would not be able to think of returning home before three months.

Puffed rice and eggs produced in Atharbari of Ishwarganj were transported by the Nasirabad train to Cumilla, Laksam, Pahartali and Chattogram. Wholesalers have also been facing difficulties since the train was suspended. Atharbari Station Master Mizanur Rahman said, “With the Nasirabad no longer operating, there is now no train at this station except the intercity Bijoy.”

When will the train resume?

A railway official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said many trains on routes that were suspended during the coronavirus pandemic were later resumed. However, the local trains on the Bhairab–Mymensingh route never returned.

Mohammad Shafiqur Rahman, chief operating superintendent (east) of Bangladesh Railway, said the Nasirabad train has mainly been suspended due to a shortage of locomotives (engines). This is temporary. The train will be resumed once the locomotive shortage eases. To somewhat reduce the difficulties in transporting goods, a luggage coach has temporarily been attached to the Bijoy Express.

Asked when the train would resume, he said, “We will have to wait.”

Mofizul Islam, president of local social organisation Bhairab Kakoli Khelaghar Asar, frequently travels to Kishoreganj by train. Expressing his frustration, he said, “The way trains are being suspended one after another, perhaps the day is not far when we will be told that there is a railway line and there are stations on the Bhairab–Mymensingh route, but there are no trains.”

item.title: Sagar-Runi murder: New clue, three more suspects identified
item.description:
A new clue has emerged in the 2012 murder of journalist couple Sagar Sarwar and Meherun Runi, with three more people allegedly involved in the killing identified, according to prosecutor and International Crimes Tribunal special investigation officer Tanvir Hasan Joha.
Joha disclosed the information in a recent media interview, saying an officer who was serving in RAB’s intelligence wing at the time has also been identified.
According to Joha, the officer told him that on the night before the murders, he had been told: “Something is about to happen. We need to be ready tomorrow morning.”
The officer was not told what was going to happen, Joha said. The following morning, he learned about the Sagar-Runi murders.
Joha said the information emerged during an investigation into allegations against dismissed army officer Ziaul Ahsan.
“While reviewing Ziaul Ahsan’s activities, we found some suspicious evidence,” he said, adding that the investigation is still ongoing.
Based on the evidence, investigators believe some individuals knew about the murders in advance, Joha said.
Asked whether Ziaul Ahsan and others linked to him knew about the killing beforehand, Joha replied, “Yes.”
He said the identified intelligence officer had initially suggested that the murders could have been linked to the BDR mutiny or another matter, but the officer is unwilling to testify in the case.
“He has said he will never give testimony in this case,” Joha said.
Investigators have also recovered two unidentified DNA samples, which Joha described as “highly important” evidence. However, it has not yet been determined whose DNA the samples belong to or whether they are from Bangladeshi or foreign individuals, he said.
Joha also raised questions about the team that went to the crime scene after the murders.
Ziaul Ahsan was heading RAB’s intelligence wing at the time, and investigators are examining whether members of the team went to the scene solely to investigate or also with the intention of destroying evidence, he said.
One member of the team has also been identified, according to Joha.
He described the murders as a “state-sponsored” killing and said such cases are difficult to resolve.
“Bangladesh Police is not so incompetent that they cannot solve a single murder,” Joha said.
Joha believes Sagar and Runi may have possessed sensitive information that could have motivated their killing and suggested that the murders were premeditated.
Sagar Sarwar and Meherun Runi were murdered at their rented residence in West Rajabazar in Dhaka on February 11, 2012.
Sagar was the news editor of Maasranga Television, while Runi was a senior reporter at ATN Bangla.
Runi’s brother, Nowsher Alam, filed a murder case at Sher-e-Bangla Nagar police station. Police initially investigated the case before it was transferred to the Detective Branch (DB) of Dhaka Metropolitan Police and later to RAB.
After more than a decade, the investigation was handed over to the Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI), which received the case documents from RAB last November.
Meanwhile, the deadline for submitting the investigation report has been postponed for the 129th time, with the court setting September 30 as the new deadline.
The report was scheduled to be submitted last Thursday, but investigating officer PBI Additional Superintendent of Police Md Azizul Haque could not submit it.
Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Ariful Islam then set the new date, according to SI Mazharul Islam of the prosecution department.

item.title: Delhi spells out Makkah Pact has security implications for India
item.description:
India on Friday said the "Makkah Pact" has security implications for India, noting that it is closely following developments that have implications for its national security.
"We continue to follow all developments that have a bearing on India's security and take all necessary steps to safeguard it," Spokesperson at the Indian Ministry of External Affairs Randhir Jaiswal told reporters in New Delhi.
He made the remarks when an Indian journalist asked about recent comments made by the Bangladesh side on the Makkah Defence Pact involving Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan.
Bangladesh’s positive stance toward the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement has triggered debate at home and abroad, amid speculation that Dhaka could eventually seek to join the pact.
The possibility will depend largely on the intentions of the three founding members - Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan - and whether they move to expand the agreement beyond its current membership.
Addressing Parliament on Thursday, Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur Rahman appeared to push back against concerns expressed over the prospect of Bangladesh joining the pact.
He described the agreement as an internal matter among Muslim-majority countries and said there was no reason for others to be concerned.
“This is an internal matter of our family, the Muslim family. Therefore, there is no scope for others to be concerned about it,” Dr Khalilur told Parliament.
He said Bangladesh would positively consider joining the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement if its existing members extend an invitation.
“We continue to closely follow developments that are happening in West Asia. This is what I have to say at this point in time,” Randhir Jaiswal, Official Spokesperson at the Indian Ministry of External Affairs, told reporters in New Delhi on August 21.
Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur said Bangladesh’s possible participation in the arrangement is not an issue at this stage, as the matter will depend primarily on the intentions of the countries currently involved in the pact. “If they express an intention to invite Bangladesh to join this pact, we will certainly have to consider the matter,” he said.
Dr Khalilur said it would be premature to discuss the advantages and disadvantages of Bangladesh joining the arrangement before any such invitation is made. “We will certainly keep all these matters under consideration,” he said.
Spokesperson at the Pakistan Ministry of Foreign Affairs recently said in Islamabad that the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement (MJDA) is a defensive framework aimed at safeguarding peace and promoting regional stability.
"As an evolving security architecture, the MJDA remains open to countries that share its commitments to collective obligations and common security interests. Any formal request will be considered in consultation with our partners in Riyadh and Ankara. The operationalization of the MJDA, however, remains at an early stage," said the Pakistani Spokesperson.
Relations between Dhaka and New Delhi have deteriorated since August 5, 2024, and the two sides have also been at odds over Bangladesh’s request for the extradition of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who has lived in exile in India since August 5, 2024.
Officials of Bangladesh and India have been in touch with each other for several weeks over the possibility of a bilateral visit by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to India.
Bangladesh reiterated that it will continue to pursue its "Bangladesh First" policy to promote friendly bilateral relations with other countries, including its neighbours, on the basis of sovereign equality, national dignity, non-interference in each other's internal affairs and mutual benefit.
On August 24, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir said Bangladesh views the “Makkah Defence Pact” involving Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye positively, noting that it would not be unusual for Bangladesh to participate in such an initiative among Islamic nations.
“We have expressed interest in the Makkah Defence Pact. So, if something happens in the Middle East, like a security pact among Islamic nations, it isn't unusual to participate. Let's see. It's being viewed positively,” he told reporters at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in response to a question.
The newly appointed State Minister said Bangladesh is now a country of recognition, with stakeholders in the Middle East and around the world showing interest in engaging with Dhaka.
“They are inviting the leadership of Bangladesh, particularly Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, to come and participate,” he said, adding that Makkah has always held a special place for Bangladesh and its people. “Makkah is in the heart of Bangladesh and in the hearts of the people,” Kobir said.
The State Minister said Bangladesh’s foreign policy has entered a new phase, with the government focusing on strengthening bilateral and multilateral relations while enhancing the country’s global visibility and influence.
Speaking to reporters at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on his first working day as State Minister, Kobir said the new responsibility is a continuation of the work he was doing as the Prime Minister’s Adviser on Foreign Affairs.
“It is not the first day of work as such. Work is about continuity,” he said, adding that the new assignment requires the government to “hit the ball… ground running.”
He said a strategic framework for Bangladesh’s foreign policy has been established over the past six months and that the government would now begin rolling out engagements based on that foundation.
Earlier this month, Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan signed a defence agreement under which an attack on one country would be treated as an attack on all three, officials said, solidifying cooperation among the three regional powers amid growing security concerns, according to the Associated Press.
The agreement was signed in the Saudi holy city of Makkah by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, according to statements issued by the three countries.
The “Makkah Joint Defence Agreement” brings together three Sunni Muslim-majority states: oil-rich Saudi Arabia, nuclear-armed Pakistan and Türkiye, which has NATO’s second-largest army and a rapidly growing defence industry.
The pact is intended to enhance cooperation and deterrence amid increased regional uncertainty and security threats linked to the war in Iran.
“The agreement is intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression, and stipulates that any armed attack against any one of the three states shall be regarded as an attack against them all,” the statements said.
It also provides for “the enhancement of all aspects of defence cooperation among the three States,” they said.

item.description:
Malaysian authorities have agreed to recruit 10,000 Bangladeshi workers completely free of cost following a special request from the Bangladesh government.
The Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Foreign Employment said this in a press release on Friday.

item.title: ASK questions police account of Rangpur family killings
item.description:
The Ain o Salish Kendra (ASK) has raised questions over the police’s preliminary account of the killings of retired teacher Ganapati Chakraborty, his wife Pritilata Chakraborty and their two children, Agami and Ayush, in Rangpur.
The rights organisation said some questions and inconsistencies have emerged between the police account and information provided by the victims’ relatives, local residents and various media reports.
ASK has particularly called for clarification over a phone call made from Pritilata’s mobile phone to her sister, Puja Chakraborty, at 2:40am and its possible connection to the suspected time of the killings.
The observations were made in a press release issued Thursday, following a two-member ASK team’s fact-finding visit to Rangpur on August 24–25.
According to ASK, the four family members were reportedly killed on the night of August 20 in Machuapara area of Kamal Kachna in Rangpur city. The incident came to light on the night of August 22 after relatives raised the alarm. Police later recovered the bodies from the house.
Following the incident, law enforcement agencies arrested two people and gave a preliminary account of the possible motive and sequence of events. However, ASK said questions remain over some aspects of the police narrative.
Puja told the ASK team that she last spoke to her sister at around 11:30pm on August 20. The following day, she noticed that Pritilata’s phone had made a call to her at around 2:40am, which she missed.
Puja said her sister normally did not call her at such a late hour, making the call unusual.
ASK said the call warrants further investigation, particularly in light of the time of the killings cited by police.
Investigators should establish who made the call, how long it lasted, the phone’s location at the time and when the family members’ phones were switched off, it said.
The human rights organisation recommended analysing call detail records, mobile phone location data and other digital evidence to verify the sequence of events.
It also stressed the need to determine whether the timing of the call is consistent with the time of the killings given in the police account.
Rangpur Metropolitan Police Commissioner Mohammad Abdul Mabud told the ASK representatives that the two arrested suspects, Siddhartha Das and Mugdha Das, had gone to the victims’ rooftop to consume yaba when Ganapati Chakraborty confronted them. Police suspect they then strangled the four family members one by one, fearing that their identities would be exposed.
Police also said the suspects allegedly ransacked the house after the killings to make it appear that a robbery had taken place and mislead investigators.
According to the police account, the suspects stayed at the house for some time after the killings, ate food and later left when the situation was favourable. Investigators identified them based on leads and evidence, and they later gave confessional statements before a court.
However, ASK said every key element of the police account should be independently verified against objective and material evidence.
The rights organisation said forensic evidence from the scene would be particularly important if the suspects had indeed stayed in the house, eaten there or taken a shower after the killings.
ASK said it should be clarified whether investigators collected and examined DNA, fingerprints, skin cells, hair and other biological or forensic evidence from different parts of the house, the bathroom, water sources, food containers, doors and windows, furniture and other surfaces.
It also said investigators should determine whether the forensic findings are consistent with the sequence of events outlined by police.
According to a fact-finding report by ASK, Puja Chakraborty said she called her sister’s phone shortly after 8pm on August 22 but found it switched off. After failing to reach other family members, she went to her sister’s house with her husband at around 9:15pm.
When there was no response from inside, they tried to enter the house with the help of neighbours. Police and Fire Service personnel later arrived, broke open the door and recovered the bodies of four family members from different parts of the house.
Puja said Ganapati Chakraborty’s body was found on the rooftop, while the bodies of Pritilata Chakraborty and Agami Chakraborty were found on the staircase leading from the second floor to the roof. Ayush Chakraborty’s body was found in a corner of a room. Furniture, clothes, jewellery and other belongings were found scattered around the house.
The ASK delegation spoke with Sanatan Chakraborty, deputy commissioner of the Detective Branch of Rangpur Metropolitan Police, who said investigators were examining various aspects of the incident and the available evidence. He also said misleading information was being circulated about the killings.
Police have suggested that the electricity supply may have been disconnected because the perpetrators feared their presence would be captured on CCTV.
ASK, however, said it was important to establish through scientific and technological evidence why and when the power was disconnected, who disconnected it and whether it was linked to the CCTV system or the killings.
Binoy Das, father of accused Siddhartha Das, expressed concern over his son’s arrest and raised questions about some details of the case, including his son’s clothes when he was taken into police custody. He called for a fair and impartial investigation.
Sena Rani Das, mother of arrested suspect Mugdha Das, also said she was unsure whether her son was involved in the killings and called for a proper investigation.
The ASK team also spoke with the parents of another suspect, Seemanta Chandra Das. They said Seemanta was at home on the night of the incident and that Siddhartha Das visited their house for some time that night but did not stay there overnight.
ASK said these statements should be verified against other information and evidence as part of the investigation.
The ASK delegation spoke with morgue in-charge Saheb Ali and Jatan Kumar, who was involved in the autopsy process.
Jatan said the bodies were in a decomposed condition and that he did not notice any marks indicating injuries from a sharp weapon. However, he said he noticed what appeared to be injuries on some parts of the bodies. He also said he did not notice any signs of sexual assault on the bodies of the two women, although samples had been collected and sent for testing.
ASK said observations by a morgue worker could not be considered a conclusive medical opinion. It said formal autopsy, chemical and other forensic reports would be the appropriate basis for determining the cause of death, nature of injuries, possible sexual violence and method of killing.
AKM Nazmul Quader, officer-in-charge of Rangpur Kotwali Police Station, told the ASK delegation that Gopinath Chakraborty, elder brother of victim Ganapati Chakraborty, filed a murder case against unidentified persons. The two arrested suspects were later shown arrested in the case, while the investigation was subsequently transferred to the Detective Branch, he said.
The case was filed as Kotwali Police Station Case No. 43 on August 23, 2026.
ASK said the accused persons’ confessional statements would be assessed through the judicial process. However, it stressed that investigators should not rely solely on confessions to establish the full truth.
Instead, it called for greater reliance on independent and objective evidence, including digital data, CCTV footage, call detail records, DNA evidence and other forensic findings.
ASK said the killing of four members of the same family was an extremely brutal incident that had caused widespread public concern. It stressed the need for a comprehensive, impartial and professional investigation to establish the motive, sequence of events and identities of all those involved.
The rights organisation noted discrepancies between the police’s preliminary explanation and questions raised by the victims’ relatives, local residents and the media. It said these discrepancies should be resolved through scientific examination of physical, digital and forensic evidence.
ASK particularly called for a thorough investigation into a phone call allegedly made from Pritilata Chakraborty’s phone to her sister Puja at 2:40am.
It also urged investigators to establish when, how and by whom the electricity supply to the house was disconnected and whether the disconnection was linked to the CCTV system, the movements of the accused or the timing of the killings.
ASK said concerns raised by the victims’ relatives over the police’s preliminary explanation should not be dismissed as baseless or misleading, but should be examined as part of the investigation. At the same time, the police version should also be independently verified against objective evidence.
Overall, ASK’s preliminary fact-finding suggests that several key questions remain unanswered despite the arrests of two suspects and police claims of confessional statements. These include the motive, timeline and method of the killings and the suspects’ alleged activities after the incident.
ASK particularly stressed the need to determine whether forensic and digital evidence corroborates the unusual 2:40am phone call and the police claim that the suspects stayed at the house, ate food and took a shower after the killings.

item.title: Nimtali Deuri – a Mughal gateway, an ascetic uprising, and Fall of Dhaka
item.description:
The only time I ever saw the Oscar-winning Hollywood actress Tilda Swinton up close was back in 2018 at the Bangla Academy premises. At a Dhaka Lit Fest session, she spoke passionately about the alternate education model followed at Scotland’s Drumduan School that she was a cofounder.
Never did I think that while exploring the historic lanes of Old Dhaka eight years later, I would come across an astonishing, full-circle connection to her ancestry.
On a July morning this year, I visited Nimtali Deuri—the grand, lone-surviving gateway of an 18th-century nawab palace located on the grounds of the Asiatic Society of Bangladesh. There, I uncovered a fascinating piece of history: Tilda Swinton's great-great-great-great-grandfather, Captain Archibald Swinton, oversaw the construction of the now-defunct Nimtali Palace over 250 years ago.
The historic Mughal-era gateway, renovated in recent years, is now under the care of the Society and houses the Asiatic Society Heritage Museum. While glancing through the artifacts, I stumbled upon archived letters, documents, and old newspaper clippings on display. They tell the tale of how Archibald Swinton, a British East India Company soldier, had to compensate a Persian-origin Bengal nawab by building him Nimtali Palace after he was evicted from his original mansion.
Built around 1765–1766, this gateway is the last standing remnant of the grand Nimtali Palace. The palace served as the official residence of the Naib Nazim of Dhaka during the transition from late Mughal rule to early British East India Company control. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
The history here is intriguing and goes much deeper than just a palace.
Nawab Alivardi Khan, who ruled Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa from 1740 to 1756, appointed Jasarat Khan as the Naib Nazim (Deputy Governor) of Dhaka in 1755. Jasarat Khan had come from Persia to seek fortune and prestige in the wealthy Mughal Subah of Bengal. He lived in the Dhaka Fort, built by Subahdar (provincial governor) Islam Khan—the Mughal governor who founded modern Dhaka in 1610. Centuries later, this same fort served as the Central Jail of Bangladesh until July 2016, when all prisoners were relocated to a newly built facility in Keraniganj.
During the second half of the 18th century, Archibald Swinton (then a lieutenant in the British forces) took over the fort in the aftermath of the Fakir-Sannyasi Rebellion—an armed uprising led by mendicants and ascetics.
The political landscape was highly volatile. After the 1757 defeat of Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah at the Battle of Plassey, the British toyed with the traitor Mir Jafar and his son-in-law Mir Qasim, awarding Bengal’s throne to one over the other. Nawab Mir Qasim held power for the better part of 1763. As relations deteriorated and war broke out between Mir Qasim and the British East India Company, the conflict caught the local administration in its crosshairs.
One of the traditional wooden louvered shutter windows on the upper floors of the Nimtali Deuri overlooks the red-brick courtyard. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
Stationed at his capital in Munger in Bihar, Mir Qasim suspected Dhaka’s Naib Nazim of showing leniency and maintaining a secret liaison with British merchants in Dhaka. On July 7, 1763, he deposed Jasarat Khan from his position and held him captive at his military camp.
On that exact same day, the East India Company officially declared war on Mir Qasim in Calcutta and reinstated Mir Jafar as the Nawab of Bengal.
At the same time, the Fakir-Sannyasi Rebellion was escalating. Triggered by the East India Company's heavy taxation, restrictions on religious pilgrimages, and the economic strangulation of local landlords, the ascetics began an armed resistance that lasted from 1763 to 1800.
Mir Qasim’s army joined forces with the ascetics, who launched a surprise assault on the British trading outpost (the factory) in Dhaka on that fateful July 7, 1763. Outnumbered and unprepared, the British staff and their small sepoy contingent abandoned their stockpiles of cloth, treasure, and ammunition to flee to Laxmipur.
This showcase exhibits historical tableware and domestic items used in 19th and 20th-century family households in Bengal. Photo Dhaka Tribune
The rebels' triumph, however, was short-lived. Recognizing Dhaka's immense strategic and commercial value, the British mobilized a massive, heavily armed punitive expedition from nearby garrisons. On July 16, they marched back toward Dhaka and on the very following day they reoccupied the city, forcing the lightly armed ascetics—who relied primarily on swords, spears, and basic matchlocks— out into the surrounding jungles.
After Jasarat Khan was dislodged and held captive by Mir Qasim, Archibald Swinton stormed Dhaka, captured the fort, and converted it into a British military residence.
Jasarat Khan, however, survived his captivity. Following the decisive British victory over Mir Qasim, Lord Robert Clive, then Governor of Bengal, released and officially reinstated Jasarat Khan as Dhaka’s Naib Nazim in 1765. As Dhaka Fort – the nawab’s original residence – no longer in his possession the Naib Nazim and his family had to take temporary shelter in the Bara Katra complex.
The artifact on display is a traditional quern-stone, commonly known as a Janta in Bengali, used for crushing grains, pulses, and lentils. Photo:Dhaka Tribune
Recognizing their prior cordial relationship with Jasarat Khan—and acknowledging that they had seized his original home—the British East India Company resolved to fund and build a suitable new palace-cum-office for him. Lord Clive instructed Archibald Swinton to orchestrate the project, selecting the northern, neem -tree-filled Nimtali ward of Dhaka as the site.
Built by 1766, the Nimtali Palace became the permanent seat for Jasarat Khan and the subsequent five Naib Nazims until the title was fully abolished in 1843.
The dramatic sequence of events—the joint attack by Mir Qasim’s forces and the ascetics, the British abandonment of Dhaka, the heavily armed counter-attack on July 16, 1763, and the subsequent British recapture of the city on July 17—was thoroughly chronicled in a letter sent from Dhaka to England on October 6, 1763.
As the Chief of the East India Company’s trading outpost in Dhaka, William Billers was required to provide the Court of Directors in London with an exhaustive account of the financial losses and security failures stemming from the July 7 assault. His October 6 correspondence serves as a crucial eyewitness record. Billers systematically broke down the dates, explaining exactly how the East India Company's factory fell, the panic that ensued, and how the subsequent counter-offensive was executed.
An authentic vintage carved wooden corbel, mounted on the gallery walls of the Asiatic Society Heritage Museum at Nimtali Deuri. They were traditionally mounted on interior walls to hold ornamental oil lamps, candles, small porcelain vases, or precious clock sets. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
A major component of the letter involved cataloging the massive loss of Company merchandise—primarily fine Bengali muslin and silk—and assessing the structural damage inflicted on the factory during the rebel occupation.
Crucially, Billers warned his superiors that these "mendicant warriors" were not typical bandits. He emphasized that they operated with deep coordination, held massive influence over the local peasantry, and possessed the tactical capability to defeat organized British outposts. His intelligence ultimately shifted British policy, prompting Warren Hastings to later launch a brutal, decades-long campaign to suppress the ascetics.
This detailed account was eventually published on May 18, 1764, in the London newspaper Lloyd’s Evening Post . The narrative of the East India Company recapturing Dhaka was also featured on February 1, 1765, in the Scottish periodical Scots Magazine .
The glass cases and illuminated backlit panels behind the writer depict scenes and figures from the Mughal era, dedicated to documenting the lineages, administrative duties, and lifestyles of the Naib Nazims who governed the region from the adjacent palace. Photo:Dhaka Tribune
I was able to reconstruct this precise historical chronology centering on Nimtali Deuri thanks to the museum's preservation of these letters, documents, and newspaper clippings. Today, these events are brought to life across the museum gallery: the Mir Qasim panel details the English abandonment of Dhaka, while the Archibald Swinton panel documents the British recapture of the city on July 17, 1763.
While the vast residential quarters, sprawling lawns, and secondary buildings of Nimtali Palace fell into ruin and vanished over the centuries, the grand archway—the Nimtali Deuri—survived. Today, this historic gatehouse stands within the premises of the Asiatic Society of Bangladesh, serving as a silent testament to post-Plassey Bengal’s volatile transition from fracturing nawab rule to British colonial dominance—a history in which Captain Archibald Swinton played a definitive part.

item.title: Civil society demands probe, justice for Rangpur family killings
item.description:
Members of civil society on Friday demanded a proper investigation and justice over the killing of retired Rangpur Zilla School teacher Ganapati Chakraborty and three members of his family.
A protest rally and demonstration was held in front of Meena Bazar at Dhanmondi-27 in Dhaka on Friday afternoon under the banner of civil society.
Speakers at the rally called for an end to killings, attacks and other acts of violence against members of the Hindu community across the country. They alleged that the killings of Ganapati and his family members were premeditated.
They also expressed concern that a powerful group may have been involved, while raising the possibility of a property dispute or the involvement of extremist groups.
Artist Kamal Pasha Chowdhury said the brutal killing of Ganapati and his family had deeply shocked him.
“We cannot remain silent until justice is served,” he said, stressing that people of all faiths must stand together against such violence.
Kamal Pasha also alleged that the organizers had received threats and intimidation attempts aimed at preventing the rally.
“We must take to the streets. We must protest every incident and build resistance. We must stand against every form of injustice,” he said.
Dr Mohammad Azizul Islam, a former official of the Department of Narcotics Control, said the killing of the Ganapati family was “extremely tragic and painful.”
“We have gathered here with one demand: the government must ensure justice for those responsible through a proper investigation into this killing,” he said.
A Hindu woman who attended the rally said members of the community no longer felt safe following the incident.
“Today it is Ganapati Sir’s family; tomorrow, perhaps we could also become targets. We want security for our lives. We demand a proper investigation and justice in this case,” she said.
At the end of his speech, Kamal Pasha Chowdhury chanted “Joy Bangla,” prompting three people to protest against the slogan.
They questioned why the slogan was being used at an event described as a social protest, saying the Awami League is a banned political party.
An argument broke out between the protesters and organizers before they eventually left the venue.
Members of the engineering community, teachers and ordinary citizens also took part in the rally.

item.title: 5,000 underprivileged people receive free eye care in Bogra
item.description:
Nearly 5,000 underprivileged people in Bogra received free eye treatment and healthcare services at a medical camp held at Bogra Poura High School and College on Friday.
The camp was organized by Al-Bashar International Foundation with support from the Ziaur Rahman Foundation, at the initiative of Dr Zubaida Rahman, Vice President of the Ziaur Rahman Foundation and a cardiologist.
Women, men and children from different parts of the district attended the camp, where they received free eye examinations, medical consultations and necessary healthcare services. Doctors also provided medicines and eyeglasses to patients based on their medical needs.
Cataract patients were identified during the camp, and arrangements were made for free surgery in cases requiring further treatment. As part of the initiative, 500 patients have been selected to undergo cataract surgery with intraocular lenses free of charge at the 250-bed Mohammad Ali Hospital in Bogra.
Former MP Helaluzzaman Talukder Lalu, vice-president of the Jatiyatabadi Krishak Dal, visited the camp. He inspected the activities, spoke with doctors and patients, and distributed medicines and eyeglasses among the beneficiaries.
Among others, Al-Bashar International Foundation Bangladesh Sector Country Director Dr Ahmed Taher Hamid Ali, BNP Central Committee member Ali Azgar Talukder Hena, Bogra district BNP leaders Fazlul Bari Talukder Belal and M R Islam Swadhin, and representatives of the Ziaur Rahman Foundation and Al Noor Eye Hospital were present.
Organizers said many low-income people cannot receive timely eye treatment due to financial constraints. The initiative was aimed at bringing essential eye care, particularly treatment for cataracts and vision problems, to those who cannot afford it.
They said such humanitarian and healthcare programs would continue in the future as part of efforts to support disadvantaged communities.

item.title: One killed, another injured in Manikganj road accident
item.description:
A motorcyclist was killed, and another rider was seriously injured on Friday afternoon after a bus hit their motorcycle on the Dhaka-Aricha Highway in Manikganj.
The accident occurred around 5pm in the Pukhuria Stone Bricks area.
The deceased was identified as Jubayer Hossain of Daulatpur in Manikganj.
According to eyewitnesses and Police, the motorcycle was traveling along the highway when a Dhaka-bound Selfie Paribahan bus struck it from behind. The impact threw both riders onto the road, causing severe injuries. Locals rescued them and rushed them toward a nearby hospital, but Hossain died on the way.
Md Harunar Rashid, Barangail Highway Police Station officer-in-charge (OC), said the driver fled the scene with the bus to the Manikganj bus stand area and escaped. Police have since seized the bus, and the body has been sent to the Manikganj Medical College Hospital morgue for an autopsy.

item.title: Meherpur worker killed in Russia gas complex blast, family mourns in grief
item.description:
A Bangladeshi worker from Meherpur’s Gangni upazila has reportedly been killed in a massive explosion at the Amur Gas Chemical Complex in Russia, plunging his family into grief.
The deceased was identified as Alal Hossain Raju, son of Kheru Mondal of Hogolbaria Mathpara village in Motmura Union, Gangni.
Alal left for Russia while his wife was pregnant. His son was born just 15 days after his departure. He was scheduled to return home next month to meet his newborn son. He will now return home in a coffin.
According to his relatives, the explosion occurred at the Amur Gas Chemical Complex in Russia’s Amur region on Tuesday, killing at least 15 people. Bangladeshi worker Zakir Hossain was among those killed, while seven Bangladeshis were injured and another remained missing.
The Bangladesh Embassy in Moscow said the complex is operated by China’s Sinopec Engineering Group. Several victims were burned beyond recognition, making identification difficult. Alal, who was initially reported missing, was feared to be among them.
The embassy said the seven injured Bangladeshi workers were being transferred from Amur to a specialised hospital in Moscow for advanced treatment, with six currently in intensive care. The embassy will oversee their treatment after their transfer.
However, Alal’s family said they learned of his death after travelling to Dhaka and contacting the Bangladesh Embassy.
“We went to Dhaka and contacted the embassy, where we were told that my brother was no longer alive,” Alal’s brother Jalal Uddin said.
“His Chinese employer also told us that Alal died in the accident and that the military had taken his body. We will be officially informed through the embassy after the legal procedures are completed.”
Alal’s cousin Mahir Uddin said he had gone to Russia 13 months ago to work at a Sinopec gas field.
“They have confirmed that he died in the explosion. His body will be brought back to Bangladesh and handed over to the family after the legal procedures are completed,” he said.
“The biggest pain is that Alal left for Russia while his wife was pregnant. His son was born just 15 days later. He was supposed to return home next month to meet his son. He will return home, but not alive—only in a coffin,” Mahir said.
News of Alal’s death has cast a pall of grief over Hogolbaria Mathpara, with relatives mourning his death and the village plunged into sorrow.
